GLQuote: Yahweh put you into my hand today
OccurrenceNote: The word “hand” is a metonym for the person’s power. “Yahweh gave me an opportunity to attack you today” or “Yahweh placed me where I could easily have killed you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: his anointed
OccurrenceNote: David speaks as if Saul were another person to show that he respects Saul because Saul is king. Alternate translation: “the one he has chosen to be king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: your life was precious in my eyes today
OccurrenceNote: Here the eyes represent seeing, and seeing represents thoughts or judgment. See how you translated similar words in [1 Samuel 26:21](../26/21.md). Alternate translation: “I have considered your life to be very valuable” or “I showed you today that I really do respect you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: so may my life be much valued in the eyes of Yahweh
OccurrenceNote: Here the eyes represent seeing, and seeing represents thoughts or judgment. Alternate translation: “so may Yahweh consider my life very valuable as well” or “so may Yahweh value my life as much as I have valued your life” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: May you be blessed
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “May Yahweh bless you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: my son
OccurrenceNote: Saul was not David’s true father. Saul speaks as if he were David’s father to show David that he wants David to trust and respect him as David would trust and respect his own father. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: David said in his heart
OccurrenceNote: Here “his heart” is a metonym that means to himself. Alternate translation: “David thought to himself” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: escape out of his hand
OccurrenceNote: The word “hand” is a synecdoche for the person. Alternate translation: “escape from him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: Saul was told
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Someone told Saul” or “Saul heard” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: If I have found favor in your eyes
OccurrenceNote: Here the eyes represent seeing, and seeing represents thoughts or judgment. See how you translated this in [1 Samuel 20:3](../20/03.md). Alternate translation: “If I have pleased you” or “If you consider me favorably” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: let them give me a place
OccurrenceNote: Since Achish was the one who would “give,” this is a metonym for “please give me a place.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Why should your servant live in the royal city with you?
OccurrenceNote: If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “I do not need to live in the city with you.” or “I am not important enough to live here with you in the royal city.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: your servant
OccurrenceNote: David speaks as if he were another person to show that he respected Achish. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: making raids on
OccurrenceNote: attacking and taking property many times (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: as you go to Shur
OccurrenceNote: Here “you” is being used as an indefinite pronoun that refers to anyone. Alternate translation: “on the way most people travel to Shur” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: Achish
OccurrenceNote: the king of Gath (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: Achish
OccurrenceNote: the king of Gath (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: your servant
OccurrenceNote: David speaks as if he is another person so that Achish will think David respects him. Alternate translation: “I” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: make you
OccurrenceNote: The word “you” refers to David and so is singular. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: he was afraid, and his heart trembled very much
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize the intensity of his fear. Here Saul is referred to by his “heart.” Alternate translation: “he was terrified” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: my life
OccurrenceNote: The word “life” represents the person. Alternate translation: “me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: torn the kingdom out of your hand
OccurrenceNote: Samuel speaks as if the kingdom were a physical object that could be held in the hand and grabbed out by another person. Alternate translation: “made you so you are no longer king” or “made another person king in your place” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Yahweh will give Israel along with you into the hand of the Philistines
OccurrenceNote: Samuel speaks as if the people of Israel were a small object that Yahweh would give to the Philistines, whom he speaks of as if they were one person. Alternate translation: “Yahweh will allow the Philistines to do whatever they want to do to you and the people of Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: will be with me
OccurrenceNote: This is a polite way to say that Saul will die. Alternate translation: “will be dead” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: Yahweh will also give the army of Israel into the hand of the Philistines
OccurrenceNote: Samuel speaks as if the army of Israel were a small object that Yahweh would give to the Philistines, whom he speaks of as if they were one person. Alternate translation: “Yahweh will allow the Philistines to do whatever they want to do to the army of Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I have put my life in my hand and have listened
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. “I could die because I listened” or “Someone could kill me because I listened” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: the voice of your woman servant
OccurrenceNote: The woman speaks as if she is another person to show that she respects Saul. She refers to herself by her “voice” to emphasize what she says. Alternate translation: “my voice” or “me speak to you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]] or [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: What are these Hebrews doing here?
OccurrenceNote: Possible ways to translate this rhetorical question as a statement are Alternate translation: (1) “You should not have allowed these Hebrews, our enemies, to be here with us.” or (2) “Tell us who these Hebrews are.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Is not this David … these years, and I have found … this day?
OccurrenceNote: Another possible translation is “Is not this David,…these years? I have found … this day.” The rhetorical question can be translated as a statement. Alternate translation: “You should know that this is David … these years. I have found … this day.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: I have found no fault with him
OccurrenceNote: This can be stated in positive form. Alternate translation: “I know of nothing that he has done wrong” or “I am very pleased with him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-litotes]])

GLQuote: He will not go down with us into battle
OccurrenceNote: The person here is a synecdoche for the army he commands. Alternate translation: “Do not let his army join with our army against our enemies” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: For how else could he make himself acceptable to his master than by taking the heads of our own men?
OccurrenceNote: If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Here “taking the heads” is a metonym for killing. Alternate translation: “The best way for David to make peace with his master would be by killing our soldiers!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Is this not David of whom they sang one to another in dances, saying, ‘Saul … ten thousands’?
OccurrenceNote: If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You should not trust David—he is the one of whom they sang one to another in dances, saying, ‘Saul … ten thousands’!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: As Yahweh lives
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. “As certainly as Yahweh lives” or “This is a true statement” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: my master the king
OccurrenceNote: David speaks as if Achish were another person so that Achish will think David respects him. Alternate translation: “you, my master and king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: it was burned, and their wives … daughters were taken captive
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “they saw that someone had burned it and taken their wives … captive” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: all the people were bitter in spirit
OccurrenceNote: The word “bitter” is a metaphor for the desire to rebel. The word “spirit” is a synecdoche for the person. Alternate translation: “all the people were ready to rebel against David” or “all the people were very unhappy” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: David prayed to Yahweh for direction
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **direction**, you could express the same idea with a clause. Alternate translation: “David prayed that Yahweh would tell David what David should do” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: you will not … betray me up into the hands of my master
OccurrenceNote: Here “hands” refers to control. Alternate translation: “you will not … violate the trust I have in you by allowing my master to control me again” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Who will listen to you in this matter?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question can be translated as a statement: Alternate translation: “No one will listen to you in this matter.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: as the share is for anyone who goes
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **share**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form. Alternate translation: “as what belongs to anyone who goes” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: against Israel
OccurrenceNote: “Israel” refers to the people who live there. Alternate translation: “against the people of Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: The battle went heavily against Saul
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. “Saul’s army began to lose the battle” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: these uncircumcised
OccurrenceNote: The nominal adjective “uncircumcised” can be translated as an adjective. Not being circumcised is a metonym for being foreigners. Alternate translation: “these men who have not been circumcised” or “these non-Israelite men” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: would not
OccurrenceNote: The ellipsis can be filled in. Alternate translation: “would not do what Saul had told him to do” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: Saul was leaning on his spear
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) Saul was weak and using the spear to support himself or (2) Saul was attempting to kill himself by falling on his own spear. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: He said to me, ‘Who are you?’ I answered him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’
OccurrenceNote: These direct quotations could be stated as indirect speech. Alternate translation: “He asked me who I was, and I told him that I am an Amalekite” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

GLQuote: great suffering has taken hold of me
OccurrenceNote: Saul’s suffering is spoken of as something terrible that has grabbed hold of him. Alternate translation: “I am suffering terribly” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: life is still in me
OccurrenceNote: This idiom means he is still alive. Alternate translation: “I am still alive” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: for the people of Yahweh, and for the house of Israel
OccurrenceNote: Both statements mean basically same thing. The word “house” is a metonym that represents the descendants of Israel. But, both “people” and “house” probably are a synecdoche representing the soldiers of Israel. Alternate translation: “for the Israelite soldiers” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: they had fallen by the sword
OccurrenceNote: Here “fallen” is a polite way of referring to being killed. Also, “sword” represents a battle. This here means “had been killed.” Alternate translation: “they had died in battle” or “enemies had killed them in battle” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Why were you not afraid to kill Yahweh’s anointed … hand?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is used to rebuke the man. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You should have feared Yahweh and not killed his anointed … hand!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: with your own hand
OccurrenceNote: This phrase refers to doing something yourself. Alternate translation: “yourself” or “personally” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: struck him down
OccurrenceNote: This idiom means “killed him.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Your blood is on your head
OccurrenceNote: Here “blood” is a metonym that implies “shed blood” and is associated with death. Here “your head” is a synecdoche referring to the man and means that he is responsible. Alternate translation: “You are responsible for your own death” or “You have caused your own death” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: your own mouth has testified against you
OccurrenceNote: Here “your own mouth” refers to the man himself. Alternate translation: “you have testified against yourself” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: Your glory, Israel, is dead
OccurrenceNote: “Your glory” refers to Saul. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the mighty
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “the mighty” refers to both Saul and Jonathan. This nominal adjective is plural, and can be stated as “the mighty ones.”(See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]])

GLQuote: have fallen
OccurrenceNote: The word “fallen” here means “died.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: Do not tell it in Gath … do not proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases mean the same thing and are repeated as part of the poetry of the song. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: so that the daughters of the Philistines may not rejoice … so that the daughters of the uncircumcised may not celebrate
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases mean the same thing and are repeated as part of the poetry of the song. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: the daughters of the uncircumcised
OccurrenceNote: This phrase refers to people who do not follow Yahweh, such as the Philistines. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Mountains of Gilboa
OccurrenceNote: David speaks directly to the “Mountains of Gilboa” as if they were listening to his song. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-apostrophe]])

GLQuote: the shield of the mighty was defiled
OccurrenceNote: The “mighty” here refers to Saul. The shield was defiled because it fell on the ground, and because the king’s blood was shed on it. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: From the blood of those who have been killed, from the bodies of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan did not turn back, and the sword of Saul did not return empty
OccurrenceNote: Saul and Jonathan are shown here to have been fierce and valiant warriors. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: the sword of Saul did not return empty
OccurrenceNote: Saul’s sword is spoken of as if it were a living thing that could return on its own. Rather than return empty, it was carrying the blood of Saul’s enemies that it killed. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-litotes]])

GLQuote: They were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions.
OccurrenceNote: Saul and Jonathan were spoken of as if they were faster than eagles and stronger than lions. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: who clothed you in scarlet as well as jewels, and who put ornaments of gold on your clothing
OccurrenceNote: “who provided you nice clothes and jewelry.” These two phrases share similar meanings that describe providing the women with expensive, attractive clothing. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: the mighty
OccurrenceNote: Here “mighty” is plural and may refer to only Saul and Jonathan, or to all of the soldiers of Israel. Alternate translation: “the mighty warriors” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]])

GLQuote: have fallen
OccurrenceNote: This is a polite way to say “have died.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: Jonathan is killed
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Jonathan has died in battle” or “The enemy has killed Jonathan” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: on your high places
OccurrenceNote: David continues to address this part of the song to the mountains of Gilboa as he started in [2 Samuel 1:21](../01/21.md). (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-apostrophe]])

GLQuote: let your hands be strong
OccurrenceNote: Here “hands” refers to the people of Jabesh Gilead. Alternate translation: “be strong” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: the house of Judah followed David
OccurrenceNote: Obeying David’s rule is spoken of as “following” him. Alternate translation: “the tribe of Judah obeyed David as their king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: they fell down together
OccurrenceNote: This is a polite way of saying they died. Alternate translation: “they both died” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: The battle was very severe that day
OccurrenceNote: It may be helpful to explicitly state that this was the large battle that followed the contest of the young men. Alternate translation: “Then the others started to fight also. It was a very fierce battle that day” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Asahel was swift in his feet like a wild gazelle
OccurrenceNote: Here Asahel is compared to a gazelle, an animal that runs very fast. Alternate translation: “Asahel could run very fast” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: seize one of the young men and take his armor
OccurrenceNote: Abner was asking Asahel to kill and plunder another younger soldier who would not be as dangerous as Abner. He did not want to kill Asahel. Alternate translation: “fight with another soldier and take his equipment as plunder” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: Why should I strike you to the ground?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is used to warn Asahel of the danger he faced. “Strike to the ground” is a polite way of saying “to kill.” Alternate translation: “I do not wish to kill you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: How then could I hold up my face to Joab, your brother?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question emphasizes that Abner does not want to fight and kill Asahel because it would destroy Abner’s relationship with Joab. Here “hold up my face to Joab” is an idiom that means that he would be too ashamed to look at Joab. Alternate translation: “I would be too ashamed to look at your brother, Joab” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: the blunt end of his spear
OccurrenceNote: This refers to the handle, which is not sharp or designed to pierce anything. It can be implied that Abner was only trying to stop Asahel from following him, and did not intend to kill him. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Must the sword devour forever?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question emphasizes that the battle had already continued too long. Here “sword” refers to the fighting. The killing in the battle is spoken of as if a wild animal was eating the soldiers. Alternate translation: “We do not need to keep using our swords to fight and kill each other.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Do you not know it will be bitter in the end?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is used to force Joab to acknowledge that continued fighting could only result in more suffering. Here “bitter” is a euphemism for the terrible suffering that would occur. Alternate translation: “You know very well that there will be a terrible result if this continues!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: How long will it be before you tell your men to stop pursuing their brothers?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is intended to convince Joab to stop fighting their fellow Israelites. Here “brother” is used to represent the members of the nation of Israel. Alternate translation: “Stop this now so that Israelites will not have to kill each other!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: if you had not said that … pursued their brothers until the morning
OccurrenceNote: This hypothetical statement tells what might have happened if Abner had not spoken wisely to Joab. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hypo]])

GLQuote: blew the trumpet
OccurrenceNote: Trumpets were used to signal orders to the armies across great distances. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: did not pursue Israel
OccurrenceNote: Here “Israel” refers to the Israelite soldiers. Alternate translation: “did not continue to chase the Israelite soldiers” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: of Benjamin
OccurrenceNote: This phrase means “from the tribe of Benjamin.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: grew stronger and stronger
OccurrenceNote: This metaphor means the number of people supporting David increased. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: grew weaker and weaker
OccurrenceNote: This metaphor means the number of people supporting Saul’s family decreased. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Sons were born to David
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “David’s wives gave birth to six sons” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Abner made himself strong in the house of Saul
OccurrenceNote: Abner’s increasing power over Saul’s family is spoken of as if he became physically stronger. Alternate translation: “Abner gained more power over the family and supporters of Saul” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?
OccurrenceNote: Ishbosheth asked this question to rebuke Abner who was acting like he was the king. Alternate translation: “You did not have the right to go in to father’s concubine!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: gone in to
OccurrenceNote: This is a euphemism for sexual relations. Alternate translation: “had sexual relations with” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: Am I a dog’s head that belongs to Judah?
OccurrenceNote: This question is used by Abner as an angry denial of Ishbosheth’s accusation. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “I am not a traitor working for David!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Am I a dog’s head that belongs to Judah?
OccurrenceNote: Abner speaks of himself as the head of a dog, which the Israelites considered to be loyal to anyone who fed them. Here “belongs to Judah” implies that Abner’s loyalty is to Judah, to which David belonged, and not to Saul’s house. Alternate translation: “Am I a traitor for Judah?” or “I am not a traitor working for David!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: into the hand of David
OccurrenceNote: Here “hand” represents the power to defeat. Alternate translation: “to be defeated by David” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: But now you accuse me of an offense concerning this woman?
OccurrenceNote: Abner asks this question to rebuke Ishbosheth. It is unclear if Abner actually slept with Rizpah, or if he was falsely accused. This could mean: (1) Abner was guilty. Alternate translation: “You should not be upset that I slept with this woman!” or (2) Abner was not guilty. Alternate translation: “You should not think that I have slept with this woman!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: throne of David
OccurrenceNote: This phrase refers to the authority of David as king. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Whose land is this?
OccurrenceNote: The original text of this question is not clear. This could mean: (1) Abner had the power to give the land to David. Alternate translation: “This land is mine!” or (2) David is chosen by God to rule the land: Alternate translation: “This land rightfully belongs to you!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: my hand is with you
OccurrenceNote: Here “hand” represents Abner’s assistance that he is offering to David. Alternate translation: “I will assist you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: you cannot see my face unless you first bring Michal
OccurrenceNote: David is stating the condition under which he will meet Abner. Here “face” refers to David himself. Alternate translation: “you cannot see me unless you bring Michal to me first” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: took her from her husband
OccurrenceNote: Paltiel was Michal’s second husband. Saul gave her to him after David fled from Saul. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: By the hand of my servant David
OccurrenceNote: Here “hand” refers to David’s power to defeat the Philistines. Alternate translation: “I will empower my servant David and” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the hand of the Philistines
OccurrenceNote: Here “hand” refers to power over Israel. Alternate translation: “the power of the Philistines” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the hand of all their enemies
OccurrenceNote: Here “hand” refers to power over Israel. Alternate translation: “the power of all of their enemies” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the people of Benjamin … the whole house of Benjamin
OccurrenceNote: Both of these statements refer to the descendants of Benjamin, who were one of the tribes of Israel. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: all Israel
OccurrenceNote: This phrase means “all of the nation of Israel.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: What have you done?
OccurrenceNote: Joab asks this question to rebuke David for letting Abner go in peace. Alternate translation: “You should not have done this!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Why have you sent him away, and he is gone?
OccurrenceNote: Joab asks this question to rebuke David for letting Abner escape. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Abner was here and you let him leave!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Do you not know … everything you are doing?
OccurrenceNote: Joab asks this question to convince David that Abner is plotting against David. Alternate translation: “Surely you know … everything you are doing.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: the blood of Asahel
OccurrenceNote: Here “blood” is associated with the death of Asahel. Alternate translation: “the death of Asahel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the blood of Abner
OccurrenceNote: Here “blood” refers to violent death. See how you translated a similar phrase in [2 Samuel 3:27](../03/27.md). Alternate translation: “the death of Abner” or “the murder of Abner” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: fall on the head of Joab and on all his father’s house
OccurrenceNote: This phrase means the results of the guilt will happen to Joab and his family as if something heavy had collapsed on them. Alternate translation: “always cause suffering for Joab and for all his father’s house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: all his father’s house
OccurrenceNote: Here “house” refers to descendants. Alternate translation: “all the descendants of Joab’s father” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: May there never fail to be
OccurrenceNote: This double negative emphasizes that there will always be someone with the problems listed. Alternate translation: “May there always be” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: is killed by the sword
OccurrenceNote: Here “sword” refers to violent death. Alternate translation: “dies violently” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: The king wept and cried loudly
OccurrenceNote: The words “wept” and “cried loudly” mean basically the same thing and emphasize how much David mourned for Abner. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: Should Abner die as a fool dies?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is used to emphasize that his death was not fair. Alternate translation: “Abner should not have died in disgrace!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Your hands were not bound. Your feet were not shackled
OccurrenceNote: These two sentences express similar ideas. They can be combined into one sentence. Alternate translation: “You were in no way a criminal in prison” or “You were completely innocent of doing wrong” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Your hands were not bound
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “No one had tied your hands” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Your feet were not shackled
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “No one had attached your feet to chains” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the sons of injustice
OccurrenceNote: This refers to people who are unjust or wicked. Alternate translation: “wicked men” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: All the people came
OccurrenceNote: This deliberate exaggeration is used to show that the nation of Israel wanted to take care of David in his grief. Alternate translation: “Many people came” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is used to show how much David respected Abner. Here “fallen” is a euphemism that means “died.” If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “It is certainly true that a great prince has died today in Israel!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: a prince and a great man
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases both refer to Abner. Alternate translation: “a great prince” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hendiadys]])

GLQuote: his hands became weak
OccurrenceNote: In this phrase “his hands” represents Ishbosheth himself. Alternate translation: “Ishbosheth became weak” or “Ishbosheth lost all strength” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: sought your life
OccurrenceNote: This idiom means “was trying to kill you.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: As Yahweh lives
OccurrenceNote: This is one of the strongest oaths David could swear, as Yahweh is the witness. Alternate translation: “I swear on the life of Yahweh” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: who delivered my life
OccurrenceNote: Here “life” refers to David himself. This means that Yahweh has kept David alive. Alternate translation: “who rescued me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: How much more … should I not now require his blood from your hand, and remove you from the earth?
OccurrenceNote: This question is used to show that the men had committed an especially serious crime. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You are even more guilty! It is my duty to require his blood from your hand and to remove you from the earth.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: require his blood from your hand
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “his blood” represents the life of Ishbosheth. Here “from your hand” represents Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, introduced in [2 Samuel 4:5](./05.md). Alternate translation: “hold you responsible for the death of Ishbosheth” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: we are your flesh and bone
OccurrenceNote: This phrase means “a relative.” Alternate translation: “we are related to you” or “we are of the same family” - (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: You will shepherd my people Israel, and you will become ruler over Israel
OccurrenceNote: These two clauses mean basically the same thing and emphasize that Yahweh had chosen David to be king. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: You will shepherd my people Israel
OccurrenceNote: Here ruling over the people is spoken of as shepherding them. Alternate translation: “You will care for my people Israel” or “You will rule over my people Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the blind and the lame
OccurrenceNote: Here “the blind” and “the lame” are nominal adjectives. Alternate translation: “those people who cannot see and those who cannot walk” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]])

GLQuote: The ‘blind and the lame’
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) this refers to people who are truly lame and blind or (2) this is a metonym that speaks about the Jebusites inside the city of Jerusalem as if they were all weak and handicapped. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: more sons and daughters were born to him
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “he had more sons and daughters” or “they bore him more sons and daughters” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: who were born to him
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “that his wives bore for him” or “he had” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: David had been anointed as king over Israel
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Israel had anointed David as king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: they all went out looking for him
OccurrenceNote: Here “all” is a generalization that means the Philistine army. Alternate translation: “the Philistine army went looking for him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: Yahweh has burst through my enemies before me like a bursting flood of water
OccurrenceNote: Here David speaks of the victory that Yahweh brought as if it were a flood of water that overflowed its banks and covered the land, causing destruction. Alternate translation: “Yahweh has overwhelmed my enemies like a flood overwhelms the land” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: When you hear … Yahweh will have gone out before you to attack the army of the Philistines
OccurrenceNote: This is the continuation of Yahweh’s instruction to David that began in [2 Samuel 5:23](../05/23.md). Yahweh here speaks of himself in the third person. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: When you hear the sound of marching in the wind blowing through the balsam treetops
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of the sound of the leaves rustling as wind blows through them as if it were the sound of marching. Alternate translation: “When the wind blowing through the tops of the balsam trees sounds like men marching” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: all the chosen men of Israel
OccurrenceNote: This metonym represents the army of the nation of Israel. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: from Baalah in Judah to bring up from there the ark of God
OccurrenceNote: It is implied that they are taking the ark to Jerusalem. Alternate translation: “from Baalah in Judah to take to Jerusalem the ark of God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: to bring up
OccurrenceNote: The word “bring” can be translated as “take.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-go]])

GLQuote: who sits enthroned over the cherubim
OccurrenceNote: You may need to make explicit that the cherubim are those on the lid of the ark of the covenant. The biblical writers often spoke of the ark of the covenant as if it were Yahweh’s footstool upon which he rested his feet as he sat on his throne in heaven above. Alternate translation: “who sits on his throne above the cherubim on the ark of the covenant” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: all the house of Israel
OccurrenceNote: This metonym represents the people of Israel. Alternate translation: “all the other Israelites with him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: anger of Yahweh burned
OccurrenceNote: Here the “anger of Yahweh” is spoken of as if it were fire. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: for his sin
OccurrenceNote: It was a sin for Uzzah to touch the ark because Yahweh had commanded that no one should touch the ark. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: How can the ark of Yahweh come to me?
OccurrenceNote: David uses this question to emphasize that he is afraid to take the ark to Jerusalem. Alternate translation: “I am too afraid to bring the ark of Yahweh with me to Jerusalem.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: King David was told
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “people told King David” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Obed Edom’s house
OccurrenceNote: Here “house” represents a family. Alternate translation: “Obed Edom and his family” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: brought up
OccurrenceNote: The word “brought” can be translated as “took.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-go]])

GLQuote: all the house of Israel
OccurrenceNote: Here “house” represents the people of Israel. Alternate translation: “all the other Israelites with him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: she despised him in her heart
OccurrenceNote: Here “heart” represents thoughts or emotions. Alternate translation: “she looked at him with disdain” or “she sneered at him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: he blessed the people in the name of Yahweh of hosts
OccurrenceNote: To bless “in the name of Yahweh of hosts” means to bless with Yahweh’s power and authority or as his representative. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: came out
OccurrenceNote: Here “came” can be translated as “went.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-go]])

GLQuote: How honored the king of Israel was today
OccurrenceNote: This is an ironic statement. Michal means the opposite of what she said, and she does not believe David acted honorably. Michal speaks disrespectfully to King David about his dancing attire and behavior. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-irony]])

GLQuote: before the eyes of the slave girls
OccurrenceNote: Here “eyes of the slave girls” represents the slave girls. Alternate translation: “in front of the slave girls” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: who chose me above your father
OccurrenceNote: Here “your” refers to Michal. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-you]])

GLQuote: over the people of Yahweh, over Israel
OccurrenceNote: Here “the people of Yahweh” and “Israel” mean the same thing. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: I will be even more undignified than this
OccurrenceNote: David is being ironic and means the opposite of what he said. He does not believe what he did was actually undignified or that his actions in the future will be undignified. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-irony]])

GLQuote: I will be humiliated in my own eyes
OccurrenceNote: Here “in my own eyes” represents what a person considers or thinks about something. Alternate translation: “I will consider myself humiliated” or “I will consider myself a fool” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: But by these slave girls you have spoken about, I will be honored
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “But the slave girls of whom you have spoken will honor me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: given him rest from all his surrounding enemies
OccurrenceNote: “given him safety from all his surrounding enemies.” Here “rest” is an abstract noun. Alternate translation: “caused the enemy people groups to stop attacking Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: I am living in a house of cedar
OccurrenceNote: Cedar is a kind of tree that is known for its strength. If you have an equivalent type of tree in your culture, you can use that name, otherwise you can reword this. Alternate translation: “I am living in a strong, permanent house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: the ark of God is staying in the middle of a tent
OccurrenceNote: Tents are temporary dwellings. If you do not have tents in your culture, you can word this differently. Alternate translation: “the ark of God is staying in a temporary place” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: do what is in your heart
OccurrenceNote: Here “heart” represents the mind. Alternate translation: “do what you think you should” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: for Yahweh is with you
OccurrenceNote: Here “with you” means God is helping and blessing David. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: the word of Yahweh came to Nathan, saying:
OccurrenceNote: The idiom “the word of Yahweh came to” is used to introduce a special message from God. Alternate translation: “Yahweh gave a message to Nathan. He said,” or “Yahweh spoke this message to Nathan:” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Will you build me a house in which to live?
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh uses a question to emphasize that David is not the one to build a house for Yahweh. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You will not build a house for me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: did I ever say anything to any of Israel’s leaders whom I appointed to shepherd my people Israel, saying, “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?”
OccurrenceNote: This has a quotation within a quotation. The direct quotation can be stated as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: “did I ever ask any of Israel’s leaders, whom I appointed to shepherd my people Israel, why they had not built me a house of cedar?” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

GLQuote: did I ever say anything to any of Israel’s leaders
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh uses a question to emphasize that he never asked any of Israel’s leaders to build him a house. Alternate translation: “I never said anything to any of Israel’s leaders” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: whom I appointed to shepherd my people Israel
OccurrenceNote: Those who are leaders of the people of Israel are spoken of as if they were shepherds and the people were sheep. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Why have you not built me a house of cedar?
OccurrenceNote: If Yahweh had asked the leaders this question, he would have been using a question to scold them for not building him a house of cedar. But, Yahweh said previously that he did not ask them this question. Alternate translation: “You should have built me a house of cedar.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: tell my servant David, ‘This is what Yahweh of hosts says: I took you … so that you would be ruler over my people Israel.
OccurrenceNote: This has quotations within quotations. It may be necessary to translate the direct quotations as indirect quotations as in the UST. Alternate translation: “tell my servant David that I took him … so that he would be ruler over my people Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

GLQuote: I took you from the pasture
OccurrenceNote: David’s job as a shepherd is referred to by the place he watched his sheep. Alternate translation: “I took you from your job as a shepherd” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I have been with you wherever you went. I have cut off all your enemies from before you. Now I will make your name great, like the names of the great ones of the earth
OccurrenceNote: This continues the quotations within quotations. It may be necessary to translate the direct quotations as indirect quotations as in the UST. Alternate translation: “I have been with him wherever he went. I have cut off all his enemies from before him. Now I will make his name great, like the name of the great ones of the earth” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

GLQuote: I have been with you
OccurrenceNote: Here “with you” means that Yahweh has helped and blessed David. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: I have cut off all your enemies
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh destroying David’s enemies is spoken of as if Yahweh cut them off, as one would cut a piece of cloth or cut a branch from a tree. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: make your name great
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” represents a person’s reputation. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: will plant them there
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh causing the people to live in the land permanently and securely is spoken of as if he would plant them in the land. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: be troubled no more
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “no one will ever trouble them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: to be over my people Israel
OccurrenceNote: To be in authority is referred to as being over someone. Alternate translation: “to rule my people Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Now I will give you rest from all your enemies … declare to you that I will make you a house
OccurrenceNote: If in [2 Samuel 7:8](../07/08.md) and [2 Samuel 7:9](../07/09.md) you translated the direct quotations as indirect quotation, then here you may need to translate “you” as “him” or “his.” Alternate translation: “Now I will give him rest from all his enemies … declare to him that I will make him a house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

GLQuote: I will give you rest from all your enemies
OccurrenceNote: “I will give you safety from all your enemies.” Here “rest” is an abstract noun. Alternate translation: “I will make all your enemies stop attacking you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: I will make you a house
OccurrenceNote: Here the metonym “house” refers to David’s ancestors continuing on as the rulers of Israel. In [2 Samuel 7:4](../07/04.md) Yahweh asked David if he would be the one to build a house for Yahweh. There “house” represented a temple. If your language has a word that can express both ideas, use it here and in 7:4. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases have similar meanings and are combined for emphasis. They both are polite ways to refer to death and dying. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: I will raise up a descendant after you
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh appointing David’s descendant is spoken of as if Yahweh would raise or lift him up. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: one who will come out from your body
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom that means the person will be David’s descendant. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: I will establish his kingdom
OccurrenceNote: Here “his kingdom” represents his power to rule. Alternate translation: “I will make him to be a very powerful king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: a house for my name
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” refers to Yahweh. Alternate translation: “a permanent dwelling for me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever
OccurrenceNote: Here “throne” represents the person’s power to rule as king. Alternate translation: “I will make his rule over Israel to last forever” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: But my covenant faithfulness will not leave him, as I took it from Saul
OccurrenceNote: The word “faithfulness” is an abstract noun that can be stated as “faithfully loving.” Alternate translation: “I will never stop faithfully loving him as I stopped loving Saul” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: from before you
OccurrenceNote: If in [2 Samuel 7:8](../07/08.md) and [2 Samuel 7:9](../07/09.md) you translated the direct quotations as indirect quotation, then here you may need to translate “you” as “David” or “him” or “his” as in the UST. Alternate translation: “from before David. David’s house … before him.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

GLQuote: Your house … before you. Your throne
OccurrenceNote: If in [2 Samuel 7:8](../07/08.md) and [2 Samuel 7:9](../07/09.md) you translated the direct quotations as indirect quotation, then here you may need to translate “you” as “David” or “him” or “his” as in the UST. Alternate translation: “David’s house … before him. His throne” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

GLQuote: Your house and kingdom will be confirmed forever before you. Your throne will be established forever.
OccurrenceNote: These two sentences have similar meanings and emphasize that David’s dynasty will last forever. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Your house and kingdom will be confirmed forever before you
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “house” represents David’s descendants, who will rule as kings. Here “kingdom” means about the same thing as “house.” This can also be stated in active form. Alternate translation: “You will live to see me establish your family and their rule over the people of Israel forever” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Your throne will be established forever
OccurrenceNote: Here “throne” represents the power to rule as king. Alternate translation: “I will cause your descendants to rule over Israel forever” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Who am I, Yahweh God, and what is my family that you have brought me to this point?
OccurrenceNote: David asks this question to express the deep emotion he felt from hearing Yahweh’s proclamation. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “My family and I are not worthy of this honor, Yahweh God.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: in your sight
OccurrenceNote: Here sight represents judgment or evaluation. Alternate translation: “in your judgment” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: your servant’s family
OccurrenceNote: Here David refers to himself as “your servant.” This can be stated in first person. Alternate translation: “my family” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: for a great while to come
OccurrenceNote: This speaks about time as if it were something that travels and arrives somewhere. Alternate translation: “and what will happen to them in the future” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: your servant
OccurrenceNote: Here David refers to himself as “your servant.” This can be stated in first person. Alternate translation: “me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: What more can I, David, say to you?
OccurrenceNote: David uses this question to emphasize that he has nothing left to say to Yahweh. Alternate translation: “There is nothing more I can say to you.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: to your servant
OccurrenceNote: David refers to himself as “your servant.” It can be stated in first person. Alternate translation: “to me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: as we have heard with our own ears
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “with our own ears” is used for emphasis. Alternate translation: “as we ourselves have heard” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: as we have heard
OccurrenceNote: Here “we” refers to David and the nation of Israel. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-exclusive]])

GLQuote: What nation is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom you, God, went and rescued for yourself?
OccurrenceNote: David uses a question emphasize that there is no other nation like Israel. Alternate translation: “There is no nation like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom you, God, went and rescued for yourself.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: to make a name for yourself
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” represents Yahweh’s reputation. Alternate translation: “to make all people know who you are” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: for your land
OccurrenceNote: Here “land” represents the people. Alternate translation: “for your people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: You drove out nations
OccurrenceNote: Here “nations” represents the people groups that were living in Canaan. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: may the promise that you made concerning your servant and his family be established forever
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “may you do what you promised to me and my family, and may your promise never change” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: your servant and his family
OccurrenceNote: David is speaking about himself in the third person. This can be stated in the first person. Alternate translation: “me and my family” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: May your name be forever great
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” represents Yahweh’s reputation. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the house of me, David, your servant
OccurrenceNote: Here “house” represents family. Alternate translation: “my family” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: is established before you
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “is secure because of you” or “continues because of you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: to your servant that you will build him a house
OccurrenceNote: David refers to himself as “your servant.” Alternate translation: “to me that you will build me a house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: that you will build him a house
OccurrenceNote: Here the metonym “house” refers to David’s ancestors continuing on as the rulers of Israel. In [2 Samuel 7:4](../07/04.md) Yahweh asked David if he would be the one to build a house for Yahweh. There “house” represented a temple. If your language has a word that can express both ideas, use it here and in 7:4. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: house
OccurrenceNote: Here “house” represents David’s family. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: with your blessing your servant’s house will be blessed forever
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “you will continue to bless my family forever” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: your servant’s house
OccurrenceNote: Here David refers to himself as “your servant.” Alternate translation: “my house” or “my family” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: David attacked
OccurrenceNote: Here David represents his soldiers. Alternate translation: “David and his soldiers attacked” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: Then he defeated
OccurrenceNote: Here “he” refers to David who represents his soldiers. Alternate translation: “Then they defeated” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: David then defeated Hadadezer
OccurrenceNote: Here both “David” and “Hadadezer” represent their armies. Alternate translation: “David and his army then defeated the army of Hadadezer” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: David killed
OccurrenceNote: Here David represents his soldiers. Alternate translation: “David and his soldiers killed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: David took
OccurrenceNote: Here “David” is probably a metonym for his soldiers. Alternate translation: “David’s soldiers took” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: King David took
OccurrenceNote: Here “David” is probably a metonym for his soldiers. Alternate translation: “King David’s soldiers took” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: David had defeated
OccurrenceNote: Here “David” is a metonym for his army. Alternate translation: “David’s army had defeated” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: David’s name was well known
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” refers to David’s reputation. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “David was very famous” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Ahilud was recorder
OccurrenceNote: A recorder was a person who spoke to the people and told them the king’s announcements. Alternate translation: “Ahilud was the herald” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: who is lame in his feet
OccurrenceNote: “whose feet are damaged.” The word “feet” here refers to the ability to walk. Alternate translation: “who is unable to walk” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: King David sent
OccurrenceNote: It is understood that David sent messengers. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: came to David
OccurrenceNote: The word “came” can be translated as “went.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-go]])

GLQuote: you will always eat at my table
OccurrenceNote: Here “my table” represents being together with David or in his presence. Eating with the king at his table was a great honor. Alternate translation: “you will always eat with me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: What is your servant, that you should look with favor on such a dead dog as I am?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question shows that Mephibosheth understands that he is not important enough for the king to take care of him. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “I am like a dead dog. I do not deserve for you to be kind to me.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: such a dead dog
OccurrenceNote: Here Mephibosheth represents the line of Saul, and he compares himself to a “dead dog.” Dogs were feral animals, not cared for, and of little importance. A dead dog would be considered even less important. Alternate translation: “such a person like me who is worthless as a dead dog” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: must always eat at my table
OccurrenceNote: Here “my table” represents being together with David or in his presence. Eating with the king at his table was a great honor. Alternate translation: “must always eat with me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Your servant will do all that my master the king commands his servant
OccurrenceNote: Ziba refers to himself as “your servant” and refers to David as “my master.” Alternate translation: “I, your servant will do all that you, my king, command me to do” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: All who lived in the house of Ziba
OccurrenceNote: Here “house” represents Ziba’s family. Alternate translation: “All of Ziba’s family” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: he always ate at the king’s table
OccurrenceNote: Here “table” represents being together with David or in his presence. Eating with the king at his table was a great honor. Alternate translation: “he always ate with the king at his table” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: though he was lame in both his feet
OccurrenceNote: “thouge both of his feet were damaged.” Here “feet” represents the ability to walk. Alternate translation: “though he was unable to walk” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Do you really think that … you?
OccurrenceNote: The leaders use a question to suggest to the king that he should not trust David. Alternate translation: “You are wrong to think that … you!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Has not David … overthrow it?
OccurrenceNote: The leaders use a question to suggest to the king that he should not trust David. Alternate translation: “You need to know that David … overthrow it.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: in order to overthrow it
OccurrenceNote: Here “it” refers to the city which represents the people who live there. Alternate translation: “in order to conquer us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: shaved off half their beards
OccurrenceNote: This act was meant as an insult to humiliate the men. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: were deeply ashamed
OccurrenceNote: Here “deeply” is an idiom that means “very.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: then return
OccurrenceNote: It is understood that they should return to Jerusalem. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: they had become a stench to David
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “become a stench” is a metaphor for “they had become offensive.” Alternate translation: “they had become offensive like a bad smell to David” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: for me, then you, Abishai, must rescue me
OccurrenceNote: Here “me” refers to Joab. Joab and Abishai represents themselves and their armies. Alternate translation: “for us, then you, Abishai, and your army must rescue us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: from Abishai
OccurrenceNote: Here Abishai represents himself and his soldiers. Alternate translation: “from Abishai and his soldiers” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: When the Arameans saw that they were being defeated by Israel
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “when the Arameans realized that the Israelites were defeating them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: They came to Helam
OccurrenceNote: Here “came to” can be translated as “went to” or “gathered at” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-go]])

GLQuote: When David was told this
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “When David heard about this” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: gathered all Israel together
OccurrenceNote: Here “Israel” represents the army of Israel. Alternate translation: “assembled all the army of Israel together” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: against David and fought him
OccurrenceNote: Here David represents himself and his soldiers. Alternate translation: “against David and his soldiers and fought them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: David killed
OccurrenceNote: Here “David” is a synecdoche for himself and his soldiers. Alternate translation: “David and his soldiers killed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: Shobak the commander of their army was wounded and died there
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “The Israelites wounded Shobak the commander of the Aramean army, and he died there” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: saw that they were defeated by Israel
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “realized that the Israelites had defeated them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: David sent out Joab, his servants, and all the army of Israel
OccurrenceNote: David sent them out to war. This can be stated clearly. Also, the word “his” refers to David. Alternate translation: “David sent Joab, his servants, and all the army of Israel to war” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: a woman who was bathing
OccurrenceNote: The woman was not on the roof, she would have been bathing outside in the courtyard of her house. Alternate translation: “a woman who was bathing in the courtyard of her house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: So David sent
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “sent” means that David sent a messenger. Alternate translation: “So David sent a messenger” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: he asked people who would know about the woman
OccurrenceNote: David was trying to find out who the woman was. The word “he” refers to David, but is a metonym for the messenger that David sent. The messenger was to ask the people for information about her. Alternate translation: “the messenger asked the people who knew her about who she was” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Is not this Bathsheba … and is she not the wife of Uriah the Hittite?
OccurrenceNote: This question gives information and can be written as a statement. Alternate translation: “This is Bathsheba … and she is the wife of Uriah the Hittite.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: took her
OccurrenceNote: David actually sent messengers, and they took her and brought her to him. Alternate translation: “they brought her to him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: she came in to him
OccurrenceNote: She came into his palace and into his bedroom. Alternate translation: “she came into the place where he was” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: he lay with her
OccurrenceNote: This is a polite way of saying that he had sexual relations with her. You may need to use a different euphemism in your language. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: she sent and told David; she said, “I am pregnant.”
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “sent” means that she sent a messenger to tell David that she was pregnant. Alternate translation: “she sent a messenger to David, and the messenger told David that she was pregnant” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Then David sent
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “sent” means that David sent a messenger. Alternate translation: “Then David sent a messenger” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: how Joab was, how the army was doing, and how the war was going
OccurrenceNote: David was asking if Joab and the army were well and about the progress of the war. Alternate translation: “if Joab was well, if other soldiers were well, and how the war was progressing” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Go down to your house
OccurrenceNote: The phrase **go down** could mean: (1) Uriah’s house was located at a lower elevation than the king’s palace or (2) Uriah’s house was of lesser importance than the king’s palace. Alternate translation: “Go to your house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: wash your feet
OccurrenceNote: This phrase is a metonym for returning home to rest for the night after working all day. Alternate translation: “rest for the night” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the king sent a gift for Uriah
OccurrenceNote: David sent someone to bring the gift to Uriah. This can be stated clearly. Alternate translation: “the king sent someone to take a gift to Uriah” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is used to show David’s surprise that Uriah did not visit his wife. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “After coming from such a long journey, you should have gone down to your house.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Israel and Judah
OccurrenceNote: This refers to their armies. Alternate translation: “the armies of Israel and Judah” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: How then can I go into my house … with my wife?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is used to emphasize Uriah’s refusal to visit his wife and can be translated as a statement. Alternate translation: “It would be wrong for me to go into my house … with my wife while the other soldiers in my army are in danger.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: to lie with my wife
OccurrenceNote: This is a euphemism. Alternate translation: “to have sexual relations with my wife” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: As sure as you are alive, I will not do this
OccurrenceNote: Uriah swears a strong promise that he will not go home to his wife as long as the rest of the soldiers are at war. He makes this promise by comparing the truth of his promise to the certainty that the king was alive. Alternate translation: “I solemnly promise that I will not do this” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: down to his house
OccurrenceNote: Possible meanings of the word **down** are: (1) Uriah’s house was located at a lower elevation than the king’s palace or (2) Uriah’s house was of lesser importance than the king’s palace. See how you translated the similar phrase “down to your house” in [2 Samuel 11:8](../11/08.md). Alternate translation: “to his house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: sent it by the hand of Uriah
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “the hand of Uriah” refers to Uriah himself. Alternate translation: “sent Uriah himself to deliver it to him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: the siege upon the city
OccurrenceNote: The word “siege” can be expressed with the verbs “surround” and “attack.” Alternate translation: “his army surround and attack the city” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: some of the soldiers of David fell
OccurrenceNote: The word “fell” is a polite way to refer to the soldiers being killed. Alternate translation: “David’s soldiers were killed” or “they killed some of David’s soldiers” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: and Uriah the Hittite was also killed there
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “including Uriah the Hittite” or “and the men of the city also killed Uriah the Hittite” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Joab sent word to David
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “sent word” means that he sent a messenger to give a report. Alternate translation: “Joab sent a messenger to David to give a report” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Why did you go so near … from the wall?
OccurrenceNote: Joab says that David may rebuke him by asking these rhetorical questions. These questions may be written as statements. Alternate translation: “You should not have gone so near to the city to fight. You should have known that they would shoot from the wall.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: shoot from the wall
OccurrenceNote: This refers to men of the city shooting arrows down at their enemy from the top of the city wall. Alternate translation: “shoot arrows at you from the top of the city wall” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Who killed Abimelech son of Jerub-Besheth?
OccurrenceNote: Joab says that David may rebuke him by asking these rhetorical questions. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Remember how Abimelech son of Jerub-Besheth was killed!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez?
OccurrenceNote: Joab says that David may rebuke him by asking these rhetorical questions. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Remember he died at Thebez when a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the top of the wall.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Why did you go so near the wall?
OccurrenceNote: Joab says that David may rebuke him by asking these rhetorical questions. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You should not have gone so near the wall!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: some of the king’s servants were killed
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “they killed some of the king’s servants” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: your servant Uriah the Hittite was killed
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “they killed your servant Uriah the Hittite” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: for the sword devours one as well as another
OccurrenceNote: Here “the sword” refers to a person who kills someone with sword. Also, killing someone with a sword is spoken of as if the sword were “eating” the people. Alternate translation: “for one man can be killed by a sword the same as another man” or “for any man can die in battle” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: she lamented deeply
