OccurrenceNote: The king uses these to phrases to emphasize that they are closely related. Being or having the same flesh is a metaphor for belonging to the same family or tribe. Alternate translation: “You are my brothers, and we have the same flesh and bone” or “You are my brothers, my close relatives” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Why then are you the last to bring back the king?
OccurrenceNote: This is the second rhetorical question here and it is also a rebuke for the elders of Judah. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You should have been the first, not the last, to bring back the king.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Are you not my flesh and my bone?
OccurrenceNote: David uses this rhetorical question to emphasize that they are related. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You are my flesh and my bones.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: my flesh and my bone
OccurrenceNote: Here David speaks of them being related by saying that they have the same flesh and bones. See how you translated a similar phrase in [2 Samuel 19:12](../19/12.md). Alternate translation: “my relative” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: God do so to me
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom that means for God to kill him. Alternate translation: “May God kill me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: he won the hearts
OccurrenceNote: Here the mens’ loyalty is referred to as their “hearts.” Alternate translation: “he won the loyalty” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: as one man
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of the men being united in their loyalty to the king as if they were one man with the same mind. Alternate translation: “and they were united together” or “they were united in their loyalty to the king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: They sent to the king
OccurrenceNote: This means that they sent a messenger to the king. Alternate translation: “They sent a messenger to the king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: in the presence of the king
OccurrenceNote: This means that the king was there and was aware of what was happening. Alternate translation: “at the place where the king was” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: call to mind
OccurrenceNote: This means “to remember.” Alternate translation: “remember” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: not take it to heart
OccurrenceNote: “To take something to heart” means to think about something seriously or to be bothered by it. Alternate translation: “not be bothered by it” or “forget about it” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Should not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed Yahweh’s anointed?
OccurrenceNote: Abishai was angry at Shimei for cursing David and is suggesting that he should be killed. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Shimei should be put to death because he cursed Yahweh’s anointed.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Yahweh’s anointed
OccurrenceNote: This refers to David. It means that he is the man that Yahweh had anointed as king. Alternate translation: “the man that Yahweh has anointed as king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: What have I to do with you … that you should today be adversaries to me?
OccurrenceNote: David uses this rhetorical question to rebuke Abishai. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “We have nothing in common with you, you sons of Zeruiah! You have no good reason to become my adversaries today.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Will any man be put to death today in Israel? For do I not know that today I am king over Israel?
OccurrenceNote: David uses these rhetorical questions to continue rebuking Abishai. These questions can be written as statements. Alternate translation: “No person will be executed today in the nation of Israel, because today I am the one who is king over all of Israel.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Will any man be put to death
OccurrenceNote: This phrase “put to death” means to be killed or executed. Alternate translation: “Will any man be killed” or “Will I order any man to die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: For do I not know that today I am king over Israel?
OccurrenceNote: Possible meanings of this rhetorical question are: (1) “I know that I am still king of Israel.” or (2) “Today I am the one who is king over Israel!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?
OccurrenceNote: David is asking Mephibosheth why he did not go with David when David and all the people who followed him left Jerusalem. Alternate translation: “Why did you not go with me when I left Jerusalem, Mephibosheth?” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: my master the king is like an angel of God
OccurrenceNote: Here David’s wisdom is compared to the wisdom of an angel. Alternate translation: “my master the king is as wise as an angel of God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: do what is good in your eyes
OccurrenceNote: This means to do what you think is right. Alternate translation: “do what you believe to be the right thing to do” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: all my father’s house were dead men before my master the king
OccurrenceNote: Mephibosheth speaks of how his relatives had deserved to be executed as if they had already been executed and were dead. Alternate translation: “all my father’s house deserved for my master the king to order them to be executed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: my father’s house
OccurrenceNote: This refers to his father’s relatives. Alternate translation: “my father’s relatives” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: What right therefore have I that I should still cry any more to the king?
OccurrenceNote: Mephibosheth uses this rhetorical question to emphasize that he has no right to request anything from the king. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Therefore, I have no right to ask the king to do anything else for me.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Why explain anything further?
OccurrenceNote: David uses this rhetorical question to tell him that he does not need to continue talking about his conflict with Ziba. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You do not need to explain this any further.” or “You certainly do not need to say any more.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: How many days are left in the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?
OccurrenceNote: Here Barzillai means that he is old and that there is no reason for him to accompany David. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “I am certainly not going to live many more years. There is no good reason for me to go up with the king to Jerusalem.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Can I distinguish between good and bad?
OccurrenceNote: Barzillai uses rhetorical questions to emphasize why he does not want to go to Jerusalem. Here “good” and “bad” refer to what is desirable and what is not. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “I cannot distinguish between what is desirable and what is not.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Can your servant taste what I eat or what I drink?
OccurrenceNote: Barzillai uses rhetorical questions to emphasize why he does not want to go to Jerusalem. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “I cannot enjoy the taste of what I eat and drink.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Can I hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women?
OccurrenceNote: Barzillai uses rhetorical questions to emphasize why he does not want to go to Jerusalem. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “I cannot hear well the voices of singing men and singing women.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Why then should your servant be a burden to my master the king?
OccurrenceNote: Barzillai uses this rhetorical question to emphasize that he does not want to be a burden to the king. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Your servant should not go with you and be a burden to you.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Why should the king repay me with such a reward?
OccurrenceNote: Barzillai uses this rhetorical question to emphasize that he does not know why the king would reward him this way. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “I do not know why the king would repay me with such a great reward” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: by the grave of my father and my mother
OccurrenceNote: This does not mean that he wants to die right next to their graves, but rather, that he wants to die in the city where they are buried. This can be stated clearly. Alternate translation: “where my father’s and my mother’s graves are” or “where my father and my mother are buried” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Let him cross over
OccurrenceNote: This refers to crossing the Jordan River. Alternate translation: “Let him cross over the Jordan” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: Kimham will go over with me
OccurrenceNote: This refers to crossing the Jordan River. This can be stated clearly. Alternate translation: “Kimham will cross the river with me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: crossed over to Gilgal
OccurrenceNote: They crossed over the Jordan River. Alternate translation: “crossed over the river to Gilgal” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: brought the king over
OccurrenceNote: They crossed over the Jordan River with the king. Alternate translation: “escorted the king over the river” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: Why have our brothers, the men of Judah … and all David’s men with him?
OccurrenceNote: The men of Israel use this question to express that they feel betrayed by the people of Judah. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “It is not right that our brothers, the men of Judah, who did not support you as king, had the privilege of bringing you and your family back across the Jordan River.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: stolen you away
OccurrenceNote: The men of Israel speak of how the men of Judah escorted the king across the river as if the king were something they stole that did not belong to them. Alternate translation: “taken you away from us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Why then are you angry about this?
OccurrenceNote: The men of Judah ask this rhetorical question to rebuke the men of Israel. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “But you have no reason to be upset about this.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Have we eaten anything that the king had to pay for? Has he given us any gifts?
OccurrenceNote: The men of Judah ask the question to express that they have not taken anything from the king. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “The king has never paid for our food, and he has never given us any gifts.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: we have even more right to David than you
OccurrenceNote: “we have a greater claim to David than you do.” It may be helpful to state clearly what having “more right” means. Alternate translation: “we have more right to serve the king and to be with the king than you do” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Why then did you despise us?
OccurrenceNote: The men of Israel ask this rhetorical question to express their anger. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You should not have despised us!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Was not our proposal to bring back our king the first to be heard?
OccurrenceNote: The men of Israel ask this question to remind and rebuke the people of Judah. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “We were the first to suggest that we bring back the king!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: We have no part in David, neither have we any inheritance in the son of Jesse
OccurrenceNote: Both of these statements mean the same thing. Sheba is emphasizing that he and the tribes of Israel have no relationship with David. Alternate translation: “The inheritance of David and his father’s family does not belong to us” or “We are not a part of David and his father’s family” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: to keep the palace
OccurrenceNote: Here the phrase “to keep” means to take care of. Alternate translation: “to take care of the palace” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: in a house under guard
OccurrenceNote: If a house is “under guard” it means that a guard is posted at the house. Alternate translation: “in a house and put a guard there” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: he did not lie with them
OccurrenceNote: This is a euphemism. Alternate translation: “he did not have sexual relations with them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: they were shut up
OccurrenceNote: This means that they were not allowed to leave the house. Alternate translation: “they were shut inside the house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: he will find fortified cities
OccurrenceNote: This means that Sheba and his men will enter these cities to hide from David’s army. The word “he” represents Sheba but refers to both him and his men. Alternate translation: “he and his men will hide in fortified cities” or “he and his men will take refuge in fortified cities” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: out of our sight
OccurrenceNote: Here David refers to his army by their sight to emphasize that Sheba and his men would be hidden and David’s army would be unable to capture them. Alternate translation: “from us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the sword fell out
OccurrenceNote: Joab let the sword fall out to fool Amasa into thinking that he Joab was unarmed, so that Amasa would allow him to walk closer to him. Alternate translation: “he allowed the sword to fall on the ground so Amasa would think he was unarmed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: he who is for David
OccurrenceNote: To be “for” someone means to support them. Alternate translation: “he who supports David” or “he who is loyal to David” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Amasa lay wallowing in his blood
OccurrenceNote: “Amasa lay squirming in his blood.” Amasa may have still been alive and rolling in his blood, but he was probably dead by this time. It is described this way to show how gruesome his body looked. Alternate translation: “Amasa lay dead in his blood” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: all the people stood still … came by him stood still
OccurrenceNote: This means they stopped walking and were staring at Amasa’s dead body. Alternate translation: “all the people stood still staring at the dead body … came by him stood still, staring at his dead body” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: After Amasa was taken off the road
OccurrenceNote: This may be stated in active form. Alternate translation: “After the man took Amasa off the road” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: in pursuit of
OccurrenceNote: This abstract noun can be stated as a verb. Alternate translation: “pursuing” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: Sheba passed through
OccurrenceNote: Here “Sheba” refers to both him and his army. Alternate translation: “Sheba and his army” or “Sheba and his men” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: battered the wall to knock it down
OccurrenceNote: This means that they used a battering ram to knock down the wall. A battering ram was a cut tree or large log with a sharpened end or an end covered in metal. It was held by several men who would pound the end against a wall. Alternate translation: “used a battering ram to knock down the wall” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: most peaceful and faithful in Israel
OccurrenceNote: This describes the cities. Alternate translation: “most peaceful and faithful cities in Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: city that is a mother in Israel
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of the importance of this city among the nation of Israel as if it were a well respected mother. Alternate translation: “city that everyone in Israel respects like they would their mother” or “city that is very important and that Israel respects” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Why do you want to swallow up the inheritance of Yahweh?
OccurrenceNote: Here the woman uses a rhetorical question to suggest to Joab what they should not do. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You should not destroy the city that is Yahweh’s inheritance!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: swallow up
OccurrenceNote: Here the woman speaks of the army destroying the city as if the city were food to be swallowed. Alternate translation: “destroy” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the inheritance of Yahweh
OccurrenceNote: Here the city is referred to as Yahweh’s inheritance to emphasize that it belongs to Yahweh. Alternate translation: “a city that belongs to Yahweh” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Far be it, far be it from me, that I should
OccurrenceNote: He repeats this phrase to emphasize that this is something he would never do. Alternate translation: “Truly, truly, I would never” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: that I should swallow up or destroy
OccurrenceNote: This refers to destroying the city. This may be stated clearly. Alternate translation: “that I should swallow up or destroy your city” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: swallow up or destroy
OccurrenceNote: Both of these phrases means to destroy. In the first phrase “destroying” is spoken of as if it were “swallowing.” These may be combined. Alternate translation: “ruin or destroy the city” or “destroy” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: has lifted up his hand against
OccurrenceNote: This means to rebel and fight against someone. Alternate translation: “has opposed” or “is rebelling against” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Give up him alone
OccurrenceNote: Joab is asking for the people of the city to release Sheba to him. Alternate translation: “Hand this man over to us” or “Give this man to us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: I will withdraw from the city
OccurrenceNote: Here the “I” refers to both Joab and his soldiers. Alternate translation: “We will withdraw from the city” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: His head will be thrown
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “We will throw his head” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom
OccurrenceNote: This means that the woman acted wisely and spoke to her people about what they should do. Alternate translation: “Then the wise woman spoke to all the people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Joab was over … Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “was over” refers to having authority over a group of people. Alternate translation: “Joab had authority over … Benaiah son of Jehoiada had authority over” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Adoniram was over
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “was over” refers to having authority over a group of people. Alternate translation: “Adoniram had authority over” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: sought the face of Yahweh
OccurrenceNote: Here “face” is a synecdoche for Yahweh’s presence. This means David prayed to Yahweh for an answer about the famine. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: What should I do for you? How can I make atonement … promises?
OccurrenceNote: These two sentences have similar meanings. Alternate translation: “What can I do to remove this sin, so that you may bless the people of Yahweh, who inherit his goodness and promises?” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: let seven men from his descendants be handed over to us
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “allow your men to give seven of his descendants to us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the one chosen by Yahweh
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “the one whom Yahweh chose” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: He handed them over into the hands of the Gibeonites
OccurrenceNote: Here “the hands of the Gibeonites” represents the Gibeonite people’s control. Alternate translation: “He gave them to the Gibeonites” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: They were put to death
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “The Gibeonites put them to death” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: It was told to David
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “Someone told David” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: who had been hanged
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “whom the Gibeonites executed by hanging” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: you do not put out the lamp of Israel
OccurrenceNote: The “lamp of Israel” is a metaphor that refers to David’s leadership and the idea that if David were to die, the people of Israel would have no clear direction. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: whose spear was like a weaver’s beam
OccurrenceNote: When a person was weaving a cloth he would run the threads through hooks attached to large sticks called a “weaver’s beam.” This means Goliath’s spear was larger than a normal spear. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: they were killed by the hand of David and by the hand of his soldiers
OccurrenceNote: Here “by the hand of” means “through” or “by.” If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “David and his soldiers killed them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: General Information:
OccurrenceNote: David’s song to Yahweh starts. He uses parallelism to emphasize what he is saying. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: out of the hand of
OccurrenceNote: This metonym means “out of the power of.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Yahweh is my rock, my fortress
OccurrenceNote: This metaphor shows a progression from a part, “rock,” to the whole, “fortress.” A fortress is built of many large rocks. This means Yahweh has the strength to protect his people from harm. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: God is my rock … He is my shield, the horn of my salvation, my stronghold
OccurrenceNote: All of these metaphors are symbols of God’s strength and power. They emphasize God’s ability to protect and save his people. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: who is worthy to be praised
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “who is worthy to receive praise” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: I will be saved from my enemies
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “he will save me from my enemies” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: For the waves of death surrounded me, the rushing waters of destruction overwhelmed me
OccurrenceNote: David compares the wicked men who wanted to kill him to flood waters that are about to drown him. These sentences have similar meanings and are used for emphasis. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: The cords of Sheol surrounded me; the snares of death trapped me
OccurrenceNote: David speaks about death and Sheol as if they are people who are trying to trap him as a hunter traps an animal. These phrases have similar meanings and are used for emphasis. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: my call for help went into his ears
OccurrenceNote: Here the metonym “his ears” refers to Yahweh and his hearing of David’s call for help. Alternate translation: “he heard my prayer for help” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: his ears
OccurrenceNote: David speaks of Yahweh as if he had ears. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: Then the earth shook
OccurrenceNote: This is Yahweh’s response to David’s cry for help from his enemies ([1 Samuel 22:7](./07.md)). David uses the imagery of the earth shaking to emphasize Yahweh’s terrible anger. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: earth shook … heavens trembled
OccurrenceNote: David speaks of the two extremes to include everything in creation. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-merism]])

GLQuote: and were shaken, because God was angry
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “because God’s anger shook them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: were ignited by it
OccurrenceNote: This is Yahweh’s response to David’s cry for help from his enemies ([1 Samuel 22:7](./07.md)). David uses the imagery of fire coming from Yahweh to emphasize Yahweh’s terrible anger. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: his nostrils … his mouth
OccurrenceNote: David speaks of Yahweh as if he had these humans parts. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: Coals were ignited by it
OccurrenceNote: Here Yahweh’s anger is compared to fire, which causes coals to ignite and burn. Alternate translation: “The flame from his mouth set coals on fire” or “He also sent burning coals from his mouth” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: He opened the heavens
OccurrenceNote: David describes Yahweh’s way of saving David from his enemies as a storm cloud gathering over a place. This emphasizes God’s power and his anger. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: under his feet
OccurrenceNote: David speaks of God as having feet like humans. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: He was seen on the wings of the wind
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “He appeared on the wings of the wind” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the wings of the wind
OccurrenceNote: This expression speaks of the wind as if it were a bird. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: rain clouds in the skies
OccurrenceNote: David describes Yahweh’s way of saving David from his enemies as a storm cloud gathering over a place. This emphasizes God’s power and his anger. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: He made darkness a tent around him
OccurrenceNote: Here the darkness Yahweh creates is compared to a tent which hides him completely. Alternate translation: “He hid himself in the darkness” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: From the lightning before him
OccurrenceNote: David continues describing Yahweh, whom he compares to a storm, coming to save him from his enemies. This emphasizes God’s power and anger towards David’s enemies. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: The Most High shouted.
OccurrenceNote: David describes Yahweh doing these actions a person would do. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: He shot arrows
OccurrenceNote: David describes Yahweh doing these actions a person would do. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: He shot arrows … lightning bolts
OccurrenceNote: David compares the lightning from Yahweh’s storm to arrows that a soldier would use. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: lightning bolts and dispersed them
OccurrenceNote: David continues describing Yahweh, whom he compares to a storm, coming to save him from his enemies. This emphasizes God’s power and anger towards David’s enemies. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Then the channels of the sea were seen … breath of his nostrils
OccurrenceNote: When Yahweh shouted in his attack against David’s enemies, it is compared to his power to create upheaval in the deepest parts of the ocean and the earth. This shows his great power and fierce anger. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: the channels of the sea were seen
OccurrenceNote: This means that the sea water moved and the ocean floor was visible. This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “People could see the channels of the sea” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the foundations of the world were laid bare at the rebuke of Yahweh, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils
OccurrenceNote: David compares Yahweh’s anger to turbulent movements of the ground. “If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Yahweh’s rebuke, the breath of his nostrils, laid bare the foundations of the world” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: out of the surging water
OccurrenceNote: David compares his enemies to a flood that threatens to drown him. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: to the measure of the cleanness of my hands
OccurrenceNote: Here “cleanness of my hands” means the same as “righteousness.” Alternate translation: “because I obey his commands” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I have kept myself from sin
OccurrenceNote: This refers to choosing not to sin against Yahweh. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: to the degree of my cleanness in his sight
OccurrenceNote: Here “my cleanness” means the same as “my righteousness.” Alternate translation: “because he knows that I have done what he commands” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: your eyes are against the proud
OccurrenceNote: Here the metonym “your eyes” refers to what Yahweh sees. This means Yahweh watches the proud person. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: you are my lamp, Yahweh. Yahweh lights up my darkness
OccurrenceNote: This metaphor compares Yahweh to a lamp, which means he gives David light and helps him to see when things seem hopeless. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I can leap over a wall
OccurrenceNote: David is exaggerating to emphasize Yahweh’s help. Alternate translation: “I can climb over the wall that surrounds their city” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: He is a shield
OccurrenceNote: The metaphor “a shield” emphasizes God’s power to protect his people. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: For who is God except Yahweh, and who is a rock except our God?
OccurrenceNote: David uses this question to emphasize that there is no God apart from Yahweh. These may be translated as statements. Alternate translation: “Yahweh alone is God. Our God alone is a rock.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: who is a rock
OccurrenceNote: David compares Yahweh to a rock to emphasize his strength and ability to protect his people. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: He makes my feet swift like a deer and places me on the high hills
OccurrenceNote: Here David’s feet are compared to those of a deer using exaggeration. Yahweh gives David the strength to move quickly and provides secure places for protection and rest. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: my hands … and my arms
OccurrenceNote: Both of these refer to David. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: the shield of your salvation
OccurrenceNote: David compares Yahweh’s power to save him to a shield that protects a soldier from his enemy. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: You have made a wide place for my feet beneath me
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh has put David in a safe place where his enemies cannot trap him. Here he refers to himself by his “feet” to emphasize his ability to stand securely. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: I devoured them and smashed them
OccurrenceNote: Here David compares himself to a wild animal. Alternate translation: “I completely destroyed them like a wild animal devouring its prey” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: under my feet
OccurrenceNote: Here “feet” refers to the power and control of victory over his enemies. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: You put strength on me like a belt for battle
OccurrenceNote: Here the strength that Yahweh gives is compared to a belt for battle that allowed David to do mighty things. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: like dust on the ground … like mud in the streets
OccurrenceNote: This means that David completely destroyed his enemies. These two phrases “like dust on the ground” and “like mud on the streets” have a similar meaning and are used for emphasis. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Foreigners were forced to bow to me
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Foreigners bowed down to me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: May my rock be praised. May God be exalted
OccurrenceNote: These sentences have similar meaning and are used for emphasis. These may be stated in active form. Alternate translation: “May everyone praise my rock. May everyone exalt God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: my rock … the rock
OccurrenceNote: David compares Yahweh to a rock to emphasize his power to protect his people. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: to your name
OccurrenceNote: Here the metonym “name” refers to Yahweh’s reputation. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the man who was highly honored, the one anointed by the God of Jacob
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “the man whom the God of Jacob highly honored and anointed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: and his word was on my tongue
OccurrenceNote: Here “on my tongue” is a metonym for David speaking. Alternate translation: “he gave me a message to speak” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: The God of Israel spoke, the Rock of Israel … me
OccurrenceNote: Here the “God of Israel” is the same as the “Rock of Israel.” The two phrases say essentially the same thing. David compares God to a rock to emphasize his power to protect his people. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: The one who rules righteously over men, who rules in the fear of God
OccurrenceNote: These two sentences both say that the king will respect God and do what God wants him to do. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: He will be like the morning light … sunshine after rain
OccurrenceNote: Here God is comparing the king to the morning light and sunshine after the rain. These are all ways of saying this king would be a delight to God and a blessing for the people. These two phrases have a similar meaning and are used for emphasis. Alternate translation: “He will be a delight to all” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Indeed, is my family not like this before God?
OccurrenceNote: Here David is saying that he agrees with God. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “My family is indeed like this before God!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Has he not made … way?
OccurrenceNote: David acknowledges that God has made a covenant with him. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “He has indeed made … way.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Does he not increase my salvation … desire?
OccurrenceNote: David believes that God will always help him and cause him to prosper. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “He increases my salvation and gives me my every desire.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: But the worthless will all be like thorns to be thrown away
OccurrenceNote: Here the wicked person is compared to useless thorns. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “But the wicked person is worthless and dangerous like thorns we throw away” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: The army returned after Eleazar
OccurrenceNote: This means that the army returned after Eleazar returned from battle. Alternate translation: “The Israeli army returned to the battle field after Eleazer had already won the battle” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Should I drink the blood of men who have risked their lives?
OccurrenceNote: David compares the water to blood because the men risked their lives to bring the water to him. He uses a question to emphasize this. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Drinking this water would be like drinking the blood of those men who have risked their lives to bring it to me.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: He was often mentioned along with the three soldiers
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “People often mentioned him when they spoke about the three bravest men” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Was he not even more famous than the three?
OccurrenceNote: This question is used to emphasize how famous he was. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “He was even more famous than the three.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: he was named alongside the three mighty men
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “people praise him like they praised the three mighty men” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the anger of Yahweh was ignited against Israel
OccurrenceNote: The word “ignite” means start a fire. Here Yahweh’s anger is compared to that of a fire. Alternate translation: “the anger of Yahweh started to burn like a fire” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Go, count Israel and Judah
OccurrenceNote: In the law of Moses, God prohibited the kings of Israel from taking a census of fighting men. The full meaning of this statement can be made explicit. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Dan to Beersheba
OccurrenceNote: This phrase uses two place names Dan, in the far north, and Beersheba, in the far south, to represent the entire country. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-merism]])

GLQuote: the king’s word
OccurrenceNote: This phrase represents the king’s command to them. Alternate translation: “what the king had commanded” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: who drew the sword
OccurrenceNote: This metonym refers to the men who were ready to fight in the army. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: David’s heart afflicted him
OccurrenceNote: The “heart” here is a metonym for David’s emotions and conscience. Alternate translation: “David felt guilty” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the word of Yahweh came to the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying,
OccurrenceNote: The idiom “the word of Yahweh came to” is used to introduce a special message from God. See how you translated this idiom in [2 Samuel 7:4](../07/04.md). Alternate translation: “Yahweh gave a message to the prophet Gad, David’s seer. He said,” or “Yahweh spoke this message to the prophet Gad, David’s seer:” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Let us fall into Yahweh’s hands rather than into the hand of man
OccurrenceNote: Here “hands” refer to power or control. Alternate translation: “Let Yahweh and not people punish us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: from Dan to Beersheba
OccurrenceNote: Here mentioning the city of Dan in the extreme north and the city Beersheba in the extreme south means the entire nation of Israel. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-merism]])

GLQuote: the angel reached out with his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it
OccurrenceNote: Here the metonym “hand” stands for the angel’s power. Alternate translation: “the angel was about to destroy the people in Jerusalem” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Now draw back your hand
OccurrenceNote: The metonym “hand” stands for the angel’s power. Alternate translation: “Do not harm them any longer” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I have sinned, and I have acted perversely
OccurrenceNote: These phrases mean the same thing and are combined for emphasis. Alternate translation: “I have sinned terribly” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: But these sheep, what have they done?
OccurrenceNote: David uses a question and compares the people to sheep to emphasize that they have done nothing wrong. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “These ordinary people have done nothing wrong.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Please let your hand punish me
OccurrenceNote: Here the metonym “hand” refers to power. Alternate translation: “Please punish me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: so that the plague may be removed from the people
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “so that Yahweh will remove this plague from the people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: what is good in your sight
OccurrenceNote: Here sight represents judgment or evaluation. Alternate translation: “what you think is good” or “what is good in your judgement” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I will not offer … anything that costs me nothing
OccurrenceNote: This can be stated in a positive form. Alternate translation: “I will only offer … something that I have paid for” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublenegatives]])

GLQuote: on behalf of the land
OccurrenceNote: Here the metonym “land” stands for the people of Israel. Alternate translation: “on behalf of the people of Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the plague on Israel was confined
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “God confined the plague that had been on Israel” or “God took the plague away from Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: old and advanced in years
OccurrenceNote: “very old.” The two phrases are similar in meaning and are combined for emphasis. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]].)

GLQuote: within all the borders of Israel
OccurrenceNote: This is a generalization. Alternate translation: “all over the land of Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: Why have you done this or that?
OccurrenceNote: This is a rhetorical question that a father would ask to discipline his son. Alternate translation: “You should know that what you have done is wrong.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: all his brothers … all the men
OccurrenceNote: This is a generalization. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: Have you not heard … it?
OccurrenceNote: The purpose of this question is to introduce the information that Nathan wants to tell Bathsheba. Alternate translation: “You do not seem to have heard … it.” or “Have you heard … it?” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: did you not swear to your servant … throne?
OccurrenceNote: The purpose of this question was to remind David of what he had promised Bathsheba. Alternate translation: “you swore to your servant … throne.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: to your servant
OccurrenceNote: Bathsheba speaks to David as if she were someone else to show that she respects David. Alternate translation: “to me, your servant” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: he will sit on my throne
OccurrenceNote: Sitting on the throne is a metonym for being king. Alternate translation: “he will be king just as I was” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Why then is Adonijah reigning?
OccurrenceNote: Bathsheba was to use a question so David would pay attention. Alternate translation: “So then, Adonijah should not be reigning.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: he shall sit on my throne
OccurrenceNote: Sitting on the throne is a metonym for being king. See how you translated this in [1 Kings 1:13](../01/13.md). Alternate translation: “he will be king just as I was” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the eyes of all Israel are on you, waiting
OccurrenceNote: Here “eyes” refers to the people. Here “the eyes … are on you” is an idiom that means the people are waiting expectantly. Alternate translation: “all the people of Israel are waiting expectantly” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: when my master the king sleeps with his fathers
OccurrenceNote: Bathsheba speaks to King David as if she were speaking about him to show that she respects him. Alternate translation: “when you sleep with your fathers” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: sleeps with his fathers
OccurrenceNote: This is a polite way of saying “dies.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: I and my son Solomon will be regarded as criminals
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “the new king will regard my son Solomon and me as criminals” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: have you said, ‘Adonijah will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne?’
OccurrenceNote: This can be stated as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: “have you said that Adonijah will reign after you, and he will sit on your throne?” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-quotations]])

GLQuote: eating and drinking before him
OccurrenceNote: Adonijah probably sat at a table where he could watch all those he had invited as they ate and drank. The main idea is that the people Nathan named were with Adonijah and they were celebrating together. Alternate translation: “eating and drinking with him” or “eating and drinking where he can see them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Has my master the king done this without telling us, your servants, who should sit on the throne after him?
OccurrenceNote: Nathan refers to David in the third person. This is a way of showing respect to the king. It can be stated in second person. Alternate translation: “Have you, my master the king, done this without telling us, your servants, who should sit on the throne after you?” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: who should sit on the throne
OccurrenceNote: Sitting on the throne is a metonym for being king. See how you translated similar words in [1 Kings 1:13](../01/13.md). Alternate translation: “who would be king after him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: he will sit on my throne in my place
OccurrenceNote: Sitting on the throne is a metonym for being king. See how you translated similar words in [1 Kings 1:13](../01/13.md). Alternate translation: “he will take my place and be king just as I was” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: May my master King David live forever
OccurrenceNote: Bathsheba knew David would not live forever; this is a way of saying that he is a good king. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: the servants of your master
OccurrenceNote: David speaks of himself as if he were speaking of someone else so Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah would remember that David is still king. Alternate translation: “my servants” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: May Yahweh, the God of my master the king, confirm
OccurrenceNote: Benaiah speaks to King David as if he were speaking to someone else to show that he respects King David. Alternate translation: “My master and king, may Yahweh your God confirm” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: has been with my master the king, so
OccurrenceNote: Benaiah speaks to King David as if he were speaking to someone else to show that he respects King David. Alternate translation: “has been with you, my master the king, so” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: make his throne greater than the throne of my master King David
OccurrenceNote: The word **throne** is a metonym for either: (1) the person who sits on the throne. Alternate translation: “make the one who sits on the throne greater than my master King David” or (2) the kingdom over which the one who sits on the throne rules. Alternate translation: “make his kingdom greater than the kingdom of my master King David” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the throne of my master King David
OccurrenceNote: Benaiah speaks to King David as if he were speaking to someone else to show that he respects King David. Alternate translation: “your throne, my master King David” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: all the people
OccurrenceNote: This is a generalization. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: is sitting on the throne of the kingdom
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) that these words are a metonym for being king. See how you translated similar words in [1 Kings 1:35](../01/35.md). Alternate translation: “is now king” or (2) that Solomon was physically sitting on the physical throne. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: a person to sit on my throne this day
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) that these words are a metonym for being king. See how you translated similar words in [1 Kings 1:35](../01/35.md). Alternate translation: “a person to be king today as I was” or (2) that Solomon was physically sitting on the physical throne. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: They stood up
OccurrenceNote: Another possible meaning is “They began to act quickly” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Adonijah … rose up, went
OccurrenceNote: Another possible meaning is “Adonijah … quickly went” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: is afraid of King Solomon
OccurrenceNote: The servants speak to King Solomon as if they were speaking of someone else to show that they respected King Solomon. Alternate translation: “is afraid of you, King Solomon” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: he will not kill his servant
OccurrenceNote: Adonijah speaks of himself as if he were speaking of another person so people will think that he respects King Solomon. Alternate translation: “he will not kill me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: not a hair of his will fall to the earth
OccurrenceNote: This is an exaggeration to say that Solomon will keep Adonijah safe. Alternate translation: “not a hair of his head will fall” or “I will keep him safe” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: wickedness is found in him
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **wickedness**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form. It is spoken of as if it were an object that could be found in a container. This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “he does what is evil” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: I am going the way of all the earth
OccurrenceNote: This is a polite way of saying “I am going to die.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: show yourself a man
OccurrenceNote: The ellipsis can be filled in. Alternate translation: “show everyone that you are a man” or “live so that everyone can see you are a good man” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: walk in his ways
OccurrenceNote: Walking on a path is a metonym for the way a person lives. Alternate translation: “live the way he commands” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: with all their heart and with all their soul
OccurrenceNote: The idiom “with all … heart” means “completely” and “with all … soul” means “with all … being.” These two phrases have similar meanings. Alternate translation: “with all their being” or “with all their energy” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: you will never cease to have a man on the throne of Israel
OccurrenceNote: The word “throne” is a metonym for the king who sits on the throne. The litotes “will never cease to have” can be stated positively. Alternate translation: “your descendants will never cease to be kings of Israel” or “one of your descendants will always be the king of Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-litotes]])

GLQuote: shed the blood of war in peace
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) “killed those men during a time of peace as if he were killing them in war” or (2) “took revenge on those men during a time of peace because they had killed people in war” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: put the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the shoes on his feet
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) Joab was close enough to these men when he killed them that their blood spattered on his belt and on his sandals or (2) the word “blood” is a metonym for guilt of murder, and the belt and the shoes are metonyms for Joab’s authority as commander, so David is saying that because Joab is guilty of murder, he should not be commander of the army. Either way, it is best to translate this literally. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: do not let his gray head go down to the grave in peace
OccurrenceNote: Here being old is represented by having gray hair, that is, a “gray head.” Alternate translation: “make sure Joab dies a violent death before he grows old” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: let them be among those who eat at your table
OccurrenceNote: The table is a metonym for the home where the table is. Alternate translation: “welcome them to eat at your home” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: do not let him go free from punishment
OccurrenceNote: This can be expressed positively. Alternate translation: “be sure to punish him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublenegatives]])

GLQuote: bring his gray head down to the grave with blood
OccurrenceNote: Blood is a metonym for violent death, and the head is synecdoche for the whole person. Alternate translation: “make sure he dies a violent death” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: slept with his ancestors
OccurrenceNote: David dying is spoken of as if he had fallen asleep. Alternate translation: “died” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: David … and was buried
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “David … and they buried him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: sat on the throne of his father David
OccurrenceNote: The throne represents the authority of the king. Alternate translation: “became king, as his father David had been” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: his rule was firmly established
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “Yahweh firmly established Solomon’s rule” or “Yahweh caused Solomon to take complete control of the kingdom” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: all Israel
OccurrenceNote: This is a generalization. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: the kingdom was given to my brother
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “Yahweh gave the kingdom to my brother” or “my brother became king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: do not turn away from my face
OccurrenceNote: Turning from the face of someone is a metonym for refusing to look at someone, which in turn is a metonym for refusing to do what that person requests. Alternate translation: “do not refuse to do what I request” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: he will not turn away from your face
OccurrenceNote: Turning from the face of someone is a metonym for refusing to look at someone, which in turn is a metonym for refusing to do what that person requests. Alternate translation: “he will not refuse to do what you request” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: had a throne brought
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “told someone to bring a throne” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: you will not turn away from my face … I will not turn away from your face
OccurrenceNote: Turning from the face of someone is a metonym for refusing to look at someone, which in turn is a metonym for refusing to do what that person requests. See how you translated similar words in [1 Kings 2:16](../02/16.md) and [1 Kings 2:17](../02/17.md). Alternate translation: “you will not refuse to do what I request … I will not refuse to do what you request” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah … as his wife
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “Allow Adonijah … to marry Abishag the Shunammite” or “Give Abishag the Shunammite to Adonijah … as his wife” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Why do you ask … Adonijah? Why do you not ask the kingdom for him also … Zeruiah?
OccurrenceNote: King Solomon was angered by his mother’s request. Alternate translation: “You are wrong to ask … Adonijah! This is the same as asking the kingdom for him also … Zeruiah!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: May God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “God will have every right to execute me—and to do even worse things to me—if I do not execute Adonijah because he has made this request” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: set me on the throne
OccurrenceNote: The word “throne” refers to Solomon’s authority to rule that was given by Yahweh. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: who has made me a house
OccurrenceNote: Here “house” refers to descendants that Yahweh gave to King Solomon, who would continue to reign after him. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the horns of the altar
OccurrenceNote: The horns of the altar symbolized Yahweh’s power and protection. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: It was told King Solomon that Joab had fled
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “Someone told King Solomon that Joab had fled” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: bury him so that you may take away from me and from my father’s house the blood that Joab shed without cause
OccurrenceNote: Here “house” stands for the descendants of David while “blood” represents guilt. Alternate translation: “bury him and so remove from me and my family the guilt for the murders Joab committed without cause” or “bury him. Do that so Yahweh will not hold me and my father’s house guilty because Joab murdered people for no reason” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: May Yahweh return his blood on his own head
OccurrenceNote: The word “his” refers to Joab. “Blood” is a metonym for murder. And, the idiom “his blood on his own head” means the person should be considered guilty for murder. Alternate translation: “Joab has murdered people, and I want Yahweh to hold him guilty for what he has done” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: more righteous and better
OccurrenceNote: These words mean basically the same thing and emphasize that Abner and Amasa were much better men than Joab. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: may their blood return on the head of Joab and on the head of his descendants
OccurrenceNote: The word “blood” is a metonym for murder. And, the idiom “blood return on the head of” means the person should be considered guilty for murder. Alternate translation: “I want Yahweh to hold Joab and his descendants guilty” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: to his house, and to his throne
OccurrenceNote: The words “house” and “throne” are metonyms for the family and the kingdom. Alternate translation: “to David’s descendants and to David’s kingdom” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: in his own house
OccurrenceNote: The house is a metonym for the land on which the house stood. The Israelites buried people out of doors in graves or tombs. Alternate translation: “where his family lived” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Your blood will be on your own head
OccurrenceNote: Here “blood” is a metonym for guilt and the head is a metonym for the person. Alternate translation: “You will be responsible for your own death” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Shimei arose
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. “Shimei quickly” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Solomon was told
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “someone told Solomon” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Did I not make you swear … saying, ‘Know … die’?
OccurrenceNote: Solomon is reminding Shimei of what Shimei had promised. Alternate translation: “You know very well that I made you swear … saying, ‘Know … die’!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Why then have you not kept your oath … you?
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) Solomon is asking for an answer or (2) Alternate translation: “You have done wrong by breaking your oath … you.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: will return your wickedness on your own head
OccurrenceNote: Here the head represents the person, and wickedness is spoken of as if it were a solid or liquid that could be put on a person’s head. Alternate translation: “will hold you responsible for all your wickedness” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: the throne of David will be established before Yahweh forever
OccurrenceNote: Here “throne of David” represents the authority and rule of David and all his descendants forever. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: in Solomon’s hand
OccurrenceNote: This use of “hand” represents Solomon’s power and authority. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: no house had yet been built
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “no one had yet built a house” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: for the name of Yahweh
OccurrenceNote: The word “name” is a metonym for the person, and “for the name” refers to worshiping the person. Alternate translation: “in which people would worship Yahweh” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: walking in the statutes of David his father

GLQuote: You have shown great covenant faithfulness to your servant
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form such as “faithful” or “faithfully.” Alternate translation: “You have been very faithful to your covenant with your servant” or “You have greatly and faithfully loved your servant” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: because he walked before you in trustworthiness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart
OccurrenceNote: Walking is a metaphor for the way one lives. The abstract nouns “trustworthiness,” “righteousness,” and “uprightness” can be translated as adjectives. Alternate translation: “because he was trustworthy and righteous, and his heart was upright” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: in uprightness of heart
OccurrenceNote: A sincere person is spoken of as one whose heart is upright. Alternate translation: “he was sincere” or “he spoke the truth and did what was good” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: have given him a son
OccurrenceNote: The “son” is Solomon. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: to sit on his throne

GLQuote: your servant
OccurrenceNote: Solomon speaks as if he is another person to show respect to Yahweh. Alternate translation: “me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: I am only a little child
OccurrenceNote: Solomon is saying that he is like a child who does not know as much as a father. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I do not know how to go out or come in
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom that means Solomon does not know how to govern as king. Alternate translation: “I do not know how to be the king” or “I do not know the right way to do things as king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: For who is able to judge this great people of yours?

GLQuote: I give you a wise and an understanding heart
OccurrenceNote: The heart is a metonym for what a person thinks and desires. Alternate translation: “I make you able to be wise and to understand many things” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: walk in my ways to keep
OccurrenceNote: Living one’s life is spoken of as walking on a path. Alternate translation: “live as I want you to live and obey” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: lay on him
OccurrenceNote: It may be helpful to state that this caused the baby to die. Alternate translation: “accidentally rolled on top of her baby and smothered him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: your servant
OccurrenceNote: The woman speaks as if she were speaking of someone else to show that she respects Solomon. Alternate translation: “I” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-pronouns]])

GLQuote: her heart was full of compassion for her son
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of the woman having a lot of compassion as if her heart were a container and compassion were a solid object. Alternate translation: “she greatly loved her baby” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: all Israel
OccurrenceNote: This is a generalization. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: the men who were subjected to forced labor
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “the men whom Solomon forced to work for him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand by the sea
OccurrenceNote: The speaker uses exaggeration to say that there were so many people that it would be impossible to count them all. The words “Judah” and “Israel” are metonyms for the people who lived in Judah and Israel. Alternate translation: “There were as many people in Judah and Israel as there are grains of sand by the sea” or “there were more people in Judah and Israel than a person could count” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Judah and Israel

OccurrenceNote: This represents the whole land of Israel from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-merism]])

GLQuote: They let nothing be lacking
OccurrenceNote: This can be expressed positively. Alternate translation: “They provided everything that Solomon needed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-litotes]])

GLQuote: God gave Solomon great wisdom and understanding

GLQuote: wideness of understanding like the sand on the seashore
OccurrenceNote: Solomon was able to understand many things about many different subjects. Alternate translation: “Solomon was able to understand many things about a wide range of subjects” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: Yahweh was putting his enemies under the soles of his feet
OccurrenceNote: To put an enemy under someone’s foot means to conquer them. Alternate translation: “Yahweh was helping David to defeat his enemies” or “David was busy since Yahweh was giving him victory over his enemies” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: for the name of Yahweh

GLQuote: Yahweh was putting his enemies under the soles of his feet
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of Yahweh giving David complete control over his enemies as putting them under his feet. Alternate translation: “Yahweh was enabling David to completely defeat his enemies” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: There is neither adversary nor disaster

GLQuote: for the name of Yahweh my God … for my name

OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “The workers constructed the foundation” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])
