OccurrenceNote: This represents Job’s feeling of being worthless. Alternate translation: “I have become as worthless as dust and ashes” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: with the strength of your hand you persecute me
OccurrenceNote: The word “hand” represents God’s power. Alternate translation: “you persecute me with your power” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: lift me up to the wind … throw me back and forth in a storm
OccurrenceNote: These expressions represent the extreme suffering that God made Job endure. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: you will bring me to death
OccurrenceNote: Here “bring me to death” represents causing Job to die. Alternate translation: “you will cause me to die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the house appointed for all the living
OccurrenceNote: Job speaks of the world of the dead as if it were a house to which God has appointed all living things to go. Alternate translation: “the world of the dead, to which everything that has ever lived goes” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: does no one reach out with his hand to beg for help when he falls? Does no one in trouble call out for help?
OccurrenceNote: Job uses these questions to justify himself for crying out to God for help. Alternate translation: “Everyone reaches out with his hand to beg for help when he falls. Everyone who is in trouble calls out for help.” or “I have fallen, and so God should not think I am doing wrong when I beg for his help. I am in trouble, so of course I call out for help!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: does no one reach out with his hand to beg for help when he falls? Does no one in trouble call out for help?
OccurrenceNote: Some versions interpret these questions as Job complaining that God has reached out with his hand to harm Job when Job was in trouble and crying out for help. Alternate translation: “Surely no one would reach out with his hand against someone who falls and calls out for help.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Did not I weep … trouble? Did I not grieve … man?
OccurrenceNote: Job uses these questions to remind God of how Job had done good to others. A: “You know that I wept … trouble, and I grieved … man!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: When I hoped for good, then evil came
OccurrenceNote: Looking for good represents hoping for good things, and evil coming represents evil things happening. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I waited for light … darkness came
OccurrenceNote: Here “light” represents God’s blessing and favor and “darkness” represents trouble and suffering. Alternate translation: “I waited for the light of God’s blessing, but instead I experienced the darkness of suffering” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: My heart is troubled and does not rest
OccurrenceNote: Job speaks of his heart as if it were a person. Alternate translation: “I am troubled in my heart and the feeling does not end” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: days of affliction have come on me
OccurrenceNote: Days of affliction coming on Job represents Job experiencing affliction for many days. Alternate translation: “I experience affliction many days” or “I suffer every day” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I have gone about
OccurrenceNote: Here “have gone about” represents living. Alternate translation: “I have lived” or “I live” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: like one who was living in the dark, but not because of the sun
OccurrenceNote: Here “living in the dark” is a metaphor that represents being extremely sad. The phrase “but not because of the sun” clarifies that “living in the dark” is a metaphor, that is, the darkness is not caused by the sun being hidden. Alternate translation: “like one who is terribly sad” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: a brother to jackals, a companion of ostriches
OccurrenceNote: Being a brother to these animals is a metaphor for being like them. Alternate translation: “I am like jackals and ostriches that cry out in the wilderness” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: my bones are burned with heat
OccurrenceNote: Here “bones” refers to the whole body, which suffers from fever. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: my harp is tuned for songs of mourning
OccurrenceNote: Here “my harp” represents Job himself, and also represents his desire to sing only songs of mourning. Alternate translation: “I play only songs of mourning on my harp” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: my flute for the singing of those who wail
OccurrenceNote: Here “my flute” represents Job himself, and also his desire to sing only songs of crying. Alternate translation: “I play only songs of wailing on my flute” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I have made a covenant with my eyes
OccurrenceNote: Job speaks of making a promise about what he would look at as though his eyes were a person and he made a covenant with them. Alternate translation: “I have made a firm promise about what I will look at” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: I have made a covenant with my eyes
OccurrenceNote: What job promised can be stated clearly. Alternate translation: “I made a promise that I will not look lustfully on a virgin” or “I promised that I will not look lustfully on a virgin” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: how then should I look with desire on a virgin?
OccurrenceNote: Job uses this question to emphasize that he would never break his promise. Alternate translation: “So I certainly will not look with lust at a virgin.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: For what is the portion from God above, the inheritance from the Almighty on high?
OccurrenceNote: Job speaks of God’s response to people’s behavior as if it were the portion of an inheritance that God gives. Alternate translation: “For how will God above respond to me? What will the Almighty on high do?” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: For what is the portion from God above, the inheritance from the Almighty on high?
OccurrenceNote: Possible meanings are Job uses this question to emphasize: (1) that God will not bless bad behavior. Alternate translation: “For if I look lustfully on a woman, God Almighty on high will not bless me.” or (2) that God will punish bad behavior. Alternate translation: “For if I look lustfully on a woman, God Almighty on high will certainly punish me.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Does not God see my ways and count all my steps?
OccurrenceNote: Here “my ways” and “my steps” are metaphors for Job’s behavior. Here “see my ways” and “count all my steps” are metaphors for knowing everything Job does. Job uses this question to emphasize that God does know all he does. Alternate translation: “Certainly God watches me and knows everything that I do.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Does not God see my ways and count all my steps?
OccurrenceNote: Job may be implying that God should know that Job is righteous and does not deserve calamity and disaster. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: If I have
OccurrenceNote: In 31:5-40 Job describes different situations in which he would deserve God’s punishment. But, he knows that they are not true and he is innocent. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hypo]])

GLQuote: walked with falsehood, if my foot has hurried to deceit
OccurrenceNote: Here “walked” and “hurried” are metaphors that represent how Job lived. Alternate translation: “done anything false or purposely deceived anyone” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: let me be weighed in an even balance
OccurrenceNote: People used balances to weigh items and to determine their value. This image represents judging honestly. It can be stated in active form. Alternate translation: “let me be judged honestly” or “let God judge me honestly” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: If my step has turned aside from the way
OccurrenceNote: Here “my step” is a metaphor for Job’s behavior, and “turned out of the right way” is a metaphor for changing from living right. Alternate translation: “If I have changed from living right” or “If I have stopped doing what is right” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: if my heart has gone after my eyes
OccurrenceNote: Here “my heart” and “my eyes” are metonyms for what Job desires and sees. The heart going after the eyes is a metaphor for desiring to do what he sees. It is implied that this refers to sinful things that Job sees. Alternate translation: “if I have wanted to do any sinful things that I see” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: if any spot has stuck to my hands
OccurrenceNote: This is a metaphor for being guilty. Alternate translation: “if I am guilty of any sin at all” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: let my crops be uprooted
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “let someone else come and take the harvest from my field” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: If my heart has been deceived by a woman
OccurrenceNote: Here “my heart” represents Job. Here the word “deceived” expresses the idea of “enticed.” The word “woman” expresses the idea of “another man’s wife.” If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “If another man’s wife has enticed me” or “If I have desired another man’s wife” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: if I have lain in wait at my neighbor’s door
OccurrenceNote: It can be stated clearly why he was waiting at his neighbor’s door. Alternate translation: “if I have waited at my neighbor’s door so I could sleep with his wife” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: then let my wife grind grain for another
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) this is an euphemism which means Job is saying may his wife sleep with another man or (2) it means she will become a slave and work for another man. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: it would be a crime to be punished by judges
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “it would be a crime for which judges would be right to punish me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: For that is a fire that consumes as far as Abaddon, and it would burn all my harvest to the root
OccurrenceNote: Job speaks of the harm that sleeping with another woman causes as if it were a fire that destroys everything. The words “that” and “it” refer to sleeping with another man’s wife. Alternate translation: “For adultery is like a fire that burns up everything from here to Abaddon and that would burn up all my harvest” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: consumes as far as Abaddon
OccurrenceNote: These words are probably a metaphor for “destroys everything so I have nothing good for the rest of my life,” but you should probably translate this literally. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: it would burn all my harvest to the root
OccurrenceNote: The word “it” here refers to the action sleeping with another man’s wife. This action is a metonym for the punishment that Job would suffer as a result of the action. A fire burning up his harvest is a synecdoche for losing everything he has worked for. Alternate translation: “those who punish me would take away everything I have worked for” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: what then would I do when God rises up to accuse me? When he comes to judge me, how would I answer him?
OccurrenceNote: Job uses these questions to emphasize that if God were to judge him, Job would not be able to make himself appear to be good. Alternate translation: “then there would be absolutely nothing I could say to defend myself when God comes to judge me.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Did the one who made me in the womb not make them also? Did not the same one mold us all in the womb?
OccurrenceNote: Job uses these questions to emphasize that he is no different from his servants. He implies that God would be angry if Job were to treat his servants as less valuable than himself. Alternate translation: “The one who made me in the womb also made them. He formed us all in the womb.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: if I have caused the eyes of the widow to grow dim from crying
OccurrenceNote: Here “to grow dim” refers to the widow having bad eyesight from crying a lot. Alternate translation: “if I have caused a widow to cry in great sadness” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: because from my youth the orphan grew up with me as with a father
OccurrenceNote: Here “the orphan” represents orphans in general. Job is describing how he truly treated orphans. Alternate translation: “because even when I was young I took care of orphans like a father” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-genericnoun]])

GLQuote: because from my youth
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “But I have done none of those things” is understood from the context. Alternate translation: “But I have done none of those things, because from my youth” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: I have guided his mother, a widow, from my own mother’s womb
OccurrenceNote: Job is describing how he truly treated widows. With the phrase “from my own mother’s womb” he uses exaggeration to emphasize that he did this all his life. Alternate translation: “all my life I have guided the orphan’s mother, a widow” or “all my life I have guided widows” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: if his heart has not blessed me
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “his heart” represents the poor man who needs clothing. Alternate translation: “if he has not blessed me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: because he has not been warmed with the wool of my sheep
OccurrenceNote: Here “the wool of my sheep” represents blankets or clothing made from the wool of Job’s sheep. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “because the wool of my sheep has not warmed him” or “because I have not given him clothing made from the wool of my sheep” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: if I have lifted up my hand against fatherless people
OccurrenceNote: Lifting up the hand against someone represents threatening to harm him. Alternate translation: “if I have threatened to harm fatherless people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I saw my support in the city gate
OccurrenceNote: Here “saw” is a metaphor for “knew,” “support” is a metaphor for “approval,” and “the city gate” is a metonym for the leaders who sit at the city gate. Alternate translation: “I knew that the leaders at the city gate would approve of me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: then let my shoulder fall from the shoulder blade, and let my arm be broken from its joint
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “then let someone tear off my shoulder from the shoulder blade and break my arm from its joint” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: If I have made gold my hope
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **hope**, you could express the same idea with the verbs “trust” or “hope.” Alternate translation: “If I trusted in gold” or “If I hoped that having a lot of gold would make me secure” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: if I have said to fine gold, ‘You are what I am confident in’
OccurrenceNote: This line means the same as the previous line. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: my hand had gotten many possessions
OccurrenceNote: Here “my hand” represents Job’s ability to do things. Alternate translation: “I have gained many possessions by my own ability” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the moon walking
OccurrenceNote: Here “walking” represents moving slowly. Alternate translation: “the moon moving across the sky” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: the moon walking in its brightness
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **brightness**, you could express the same idea with the words “bright” or “brightly.” Alternate translation: “the bright moon moving across the sky” or “the moon moving brightly across the sky” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: if my heart has been secretly attracted
OccurrenceNote: Here “my heart” represents Job. This phrase can be stated in active form. Alternate translation: “if I have been secretly attracted to them” or “if I have secretly desired to worship them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: to be punished by judges
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “for which judges would be right to punish me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: at the destruction of anyone who hated me
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **destruction**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form such as “destroy.” Alternate translation: “when anyone who hated me was destroyed” or “when bad things happened to anyone who hated me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: Indeed, I have not even allowed my mouth to sin
OccurrenceNote: Here “my mouth” represents Job speaking. Alternate translation: “Truly I did not let myself sin” or “Truly, I did not sin” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: by asking for his life with a curse
OccurrenceNote: Here “asking for his life with a curse” represents cursing someone’s life so that he will die. Alternate translation: “by cursing him so that he would die” or “by cursing his life” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the men of my tent
OccurrenceNote: The tent represents Job’s household. The men of his tent includes family members and servants. All of these knew Job well. Alternate translation: “the men of my household” or “my family members and servants” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Who can find one who has not been filled with Job’s food?
OccurrenceNote: Job’s men would have used this question to emphasize that Job was generous to everyone. Alternate translation: “Everyone has been filled with Job’s food!” or “Everyone we know of has eaten as much of Job’s food as he wanted!”(See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: even the foreigner has never had to stay in the city square
OccurrenceNote: Job is explaining how he truly treated foreigners. Here “stay in the city square” represents sleeping overnight in the city square. Alternate translation: “foreigners have never had to sleep in the city square” or “foreigners have never had to sleep outside” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I have always opened my doors to the traveler
OccurrenceNote: Here “opened my doors to the traveler” represents welcoming the traveler into his home. Alternate translation: “I have always welcomed the traveler into my home” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: If … I have hidden my sins
OccurrenceNote: Here “have hidden my sins” represents trying to keep people from knowing that he had sinned. Alternate translation: “If … I have tried to keep my sins a secret” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: by hiding my guilt inside my tunic
OccurrenceNote: This represents trying to keep people from knowing that he is guilty. Alternate translation: “by hiding the evidence of my guilt inside my tunic” or “like one who hides the evidence of his guilt inside his tunic” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: because I feared the great multitude, because the contempt of families terrified me
OccurrenceNote: This would be the reason for hiding his sins. These mean the same thing. They emphasize that a person may hide his sin because he fears what other people may think about him. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Oh, if only I had someone to hear me!
OccurrenceNote: This exclamation expresses Job’s wish. Alternate translation: “I wish I had someone to hear me” or “I wish that someone would listen to me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-exclamations]])

GLQuote: here is my signature
OccurrenceNote: Here “my signature” represents Job’s promise that everything he is saying is true. He speaks of his complaint as if he had written a legal document. Alternate translation: “I solemnly promise that all I have said is true” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: let the Almighty answer me!
OccurrenceNote: Here an answer probably refers to telling Job what wrong he accuses Job of doing. Alternate translation: “let the Almighty tell me what I have done wrong” or “I wish the Almighty would say what I have done wrong” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Surely I would carry it openly on my shoulder; I would put it on like a crown
OccurrenceNote: This represents putting it where everyone could read it. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I would declare to him an accounting for my steps
OccurrenceNote: Here “my steps” represents Job’s actions. Alternate translation: “I would declare to him an accounting for all I have done” or “I would tell him everything I have done” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: as a confident prince I would go up to him
OccurrenceNote: This means Job would approach God without any fear. Job implies that he could do this because he was not guilty. Alternate translation: “I would approach him boldly” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: General Information:
OccurrenceNote: This concludes Job’s description of situations in which he would deserve God’s punishment, but he knows they are not true. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hypo]])

GLQuote: If my land ever cries out against me, and its furrows weep together
OccurrenceNote: Job speaks of being guilty as if his land were a person who cries out against Job because of the wrong Job has done to the land. Alternate translation: “If I have done wrong concerning my land” or “If I have stolen my land from someone” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: to lose their lives
OccurrenceNote: This represents dying. Alternate translation: “to die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: weeds instead of barley
OccurrenceNote: The words “let” and “grow” are understood from the previous phrase. Alternate translation: “let weeds grow instead of barley” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: he was righteous in his own eyes
OccurrenceNote: The eyes represent seeing, and seeing represents thoughts or judgment. Alternate translation: “he considered himself righteous” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Then was kindled the anger of Elihu son of Barakel the Buzite, of the family of Ram; it was kindled against Job
OccurrenceNote: This compares Elihu’s anger to someone starting a fire. Also, If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Then Elihu son of Barakel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, became very angry with Job” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: he justified himself rather than God
OccurrenceNote: This means that he considered himself innocent and believed God had been wrong to punish him. Alternate translation: “he justified himself and claimed that God had been wrong to punish him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Elihu’s anger was also kindled against his three friends
OccurrenceNote: This compares Elihu’s anger to someone starting a fire. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Elihu also became very angry with his three friends” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: that there was no answer in the mouths of these three men
OccurrenceNote: This means that the men were done speaking to Job. This speaks of the men possibly having an answer as if the answer were an object that would be in their mouths. Alternate translation: “that these three men had nothing else to say” or “that these three men had no more answers to give Job” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: his anger was kindled
OccurrenceNote: This compares Elihu’s anger to someone starting a fire. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “he became very angry” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: you are very old
OccurrenceNote: Here “you” is plural and refers to Job and his three friends. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-you]])

GLQuote: Length of days should speak; a multitude of years should teach wisdom
OccurrenceNote: These two lines mean the same thing. Elihu emphasizes that since older people are wiser than younger people, they should be the first to speak of what they know. Alternate translation: “He who has lived many years should speak; He would is older should teach wisdom” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: there is a spirit in a man; the breath of the Almighty
OccurrenceNote: Both phrases mean the same thing. Elihu is emphasizing that a man’s wisdom comes from God. Alternate translation: “there is a spirit in a man, that is, the breath of the Almighty that” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: the breath of the Almighty
OccurrenceNote: Here the spirit is represented by “breath.” Alternate translation: “the spirit of the Almighty” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I waited for your words
OccurrenceNote: “I waited to hear what you would say.” The word “your” refers to Job’s friends. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-you]])

GLQuote: to defeat Job
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of God responding to Job and correcting him as if he were defeating him in battle. Alternate translation: “to refute Job” or “to answer Job” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Should I wait because they are not speaking, because they stand there silent and answer no more?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu uses a question to emphasize that he will not wait any longer to speak. Elihu answers this question himself in the next verse. Alternate translation: But because you do not speak, I certainly will not wait any longer; you merely stand there and do not reply anymore. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: I am full of words
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of having a lot to say as being full of words. Alternate translation: “I have so much to say” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: my breast is like fermenting wine that has no vent; like new wineskins, it is ready to burst
OccurrenceNote: While wine is fermenting, gas collects in the container. If the gas is not let out the container will burst. Elihu means that he has so much to say that if he does not speak he feels like he will burst. Also, these two phrases are parallel and have the same meaning. Alternate translation: “I feel like my breast is about to burst, like a container of fermenting wine that has no vent” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: my breast is
OccurrenceNote: This represents Elihu, specifically his spirit. Alternate translation: “my spirit is” or “I am” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: I may be refreshed
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “I may feel better” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: open my lips
OccurrenceNote: Here the “lips” represent the mouth. Alternate translation: “open my mouth” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: take me away
OccurrenceNote: This means that he would destroy him. Alternate translation: “destroy me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: hear my speech; listen to all my words
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases mean the same thing. Elihu is emphasizing that Job must listen carefully. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: I have opened my mouth … my tongue has spoken in my mouth
OccurrenceNote: These mean the same thing. Elihu is emphasizing that he is now ready to speak. His “tongue” speaking represents himself speaking. Alternate translation: “I have opened my mouth and I have begun to speak” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: My words come from the uprightness of my heart
OccurrenceNote: Here Elihu refers to himself by his “heart” as he speaks of being upright. Alternate translation: “I will speak with uprightness” or “I will speak with complete honesty” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: my lips speak pure knowledge
OccurrenceNote: Here Elihu refers to himself by his “lips” to emphasize his speech. Alternate translation: “I will speak sincerely to you the things I know” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: The Spirit of God … has given me life
OccurrenceNote: These two lines mean the same thing. Elihu is emphasizing that God has made him and so gives authority to what he is saying. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: set your words in order before me and stand up
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of Job preparing what he will say as if he were setting up and organizing physical objects. Alternate translation: “prepare what you will say, and stand up and answer me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I am just as you are in God’s sight
OccurrenceNote: Here sight represents judgment or evaluation. Alternate translation: “I am just as you are in God’s judgment” or “God judges me the same way that he judges you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I also have been formed out of the clay
OccurrenceNote: Though people are not made out of clay, God has made everyone as a potter carefully makes things out of clay. Alternate translation: “God has made both of us just as a potter forms things from clay” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I also have been formed
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “God has also made me” or “God has formed both of us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: neither will my pressure be heavy upon you
OccurrenceNote: This means that he will not hinder Job or burden him. He speaks of emotional burden here as if it were a heavy physical burden. Alternate translation: “neither will I burden you” or “I will not oppress you with what I say” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: clean
OccurrenceNote: A person who God considers spiritually acceptable is spoken of as if the person were physically clean. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: He puts my feet in stocks
OccurrenceNote: “Stocks” are wooden blocks a jailer puts around a prisoner’s feet to restrict his movement. Job speaks of feeling like he is a prisoner by saying that he is in stocks. Alternate translation: “I feel he has made me a prisoner” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: my paths
OccurrenceNote: These words refer to where he goes. Here where he goes represents what he does. Alternate translation: “everything that I do” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Why do you struggle against him?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu uses this question to emphasize that Job should not struggle against God. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “You should not struggle against God.” or “You should not try to argue with God.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: God speaks once—yes, twice
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “God speaks again and again in different ways” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: a dream … a vision of the night
OccurrenceNote: These phrases have the same meaning. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: when deep sleep falls upon men, in slumber on the bed
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of people being in a deep sleep as if the sleep fell upon them or overcame them. Alternate translation: “when people are fully asleep on their bed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: then God opens the ears of men
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of God making people aware of things as if he were opening their ears so that they could hear. Alternate translation: “then God reveals things to people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: in order to pull man back from
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of God keeping someone from doing something as if he were physically pulling him away from harm. Alternate translation: “in order to keep him from” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: God keeps man’s life back from the pit … his life from crossing over to death
OccurrenceNote: Both of these statements mean the same thing. Alternate translation: “God saves people from the grave and from death” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: the pit
OccurrenceNote: The place where people go when they die is referred to here as “the pit.” Alternate translation: “the place where dead people are” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: man’s life back … his life
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “man from dying and … he keeps him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: from crossing over to death
OccurrenceNote: Here “death” represents the place where people go when they die, that is, sheol. Alternate translation: “from going to sheol” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Man is punished also
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “God also punishes a person” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: with pain on his bed
OccurrenceNote: This means that the person is experiencing such pain that he must lie in bed. Alternate translation: “with pain so that he must lie in bed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: so that his life abhors food, and his soul abhors delicacies
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases mean basically the same thing, that the person is in so much pain that he cannot even eat. The person is represented by his “life” and his “soul.” Alternate translation: “the result is that he does not desire any food, not even very special food” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: His flesh is consumed away so that it cannot be seen; his bones, once not seen, now stick out
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. “His flesh” refers to his fat and muscles, not to his body’s outer skin. Alternate translation: “Disease makes his body weak and thin so that a person can see his bones” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: his soul draws close to the pit
OccurrenceNote: Here a person is represented by his “soul.” Alternate translation: “he is close to going into the grave” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: the pit
OccurrenceNote: The place where people go when they die is referred to here as “the pit.” Alternate translation: “the place where dead people are” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: his life to those who wish to destroy it
OccurrenceNote: Here the person is represented by his “life.” The phrase “those who wish to destroy it” refers to the place where people go after they die. Alternate translation: “and he is close to going to the place where dead people go” or “and he will soon go to the place of the dead” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the pit
OccurrenceNote: The place where people go when they die is referred to here as “the pit.” Alternate translation: “the place where dead people are” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I have found a ransom for him
OccurrenceNote: This means that the angel has found a way to pay for the sins of the man so that he does not have to die. Alternate translation: “for I have found a way for you to keep him from dying” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: his flesh will become fresher than a child’s
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of the man being healed and his body growing strong again as if his body became new like a child’s body. Alternate translation: “the sick man’s body will become new again like a young person’s body” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: fresher than a child’s
OccurrenceNote: In this comparison, the word “fresher” is an exaggeration. Alternate translation: “fresh like a child’s” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: a child’s
OccurrenceNote: This refers to a child’s flesh. Alternate translation: “a child’s flesh” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: it is restored to the days of his youth
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of the man’s flesh again being as strong as it was when he was young. Alternate translation: “it will become strong again, as it was when he was young” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: he sees God’s face with joy
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “he joyfully worships God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: God’s face
OccurrenceNote: Here God is represented by his “face.” Alternate translation: “God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: but my sin was not punished
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “but God did not punish me for sinning” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: rescued my soul from going down into the pit
OccurrenceNote: Here the person is referred to by his “soul.” Alternate translation: “rescued me from dying and going to the pit” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: the pit
OccurrenceNote: The place where people go when they die is referred to here as “the pit.” Alternate translation: “the place where dead people are” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: my life will continue to see light
OccurrenceNote: Here the person is represented by his “life.” Also, living is spoken of as seeing the light. Alternate translation: “I will continue to live and see the daylight” or “I will continue to live” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: twice, yes, even three times
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “again and again” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: his soul
OccurrenceNote: The person is represented by his “soul.” Alternate translation: “him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: to bring his soul back from the pit
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of saving the man from dying as if he had died and was being brought back to life. Alternate translation: “to keep him from dying and going to the pit” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the pit
OccurrenceNote: The place where people go when they die is referred to here as “the pit.” Alternate translation: “the place where dead people are” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: he may be enlightened with the light of life
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom and may be stated in active form. Alternate translation: “he may be happy to still be alive” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Pay attention, Job, and listen to me
OccurrenceNote: These phrases mean the same thing. Alternate translation: “Listen carefully to me, Job” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: that you are in the right
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “that you are innocent” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: you wise men … you who have knowledge
OccurrenceNote: Elihu is criticizing Job and his friends. He does not think they are actually wise. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-irony]])

GLQuote: For the ear tries words as the palate tastes food
OccurrenceNote: Elihu means people listen carefully to determine what is right or wrong just like we taste food to determine if it is good or bad. Here people are referred to by their “ear” and their “palate” to emphasize that they are tasting and hearing. Alternate translation: “For we listen to words to know what is good and bad, just as we taste foods to know what is good to eat” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: Let us
OccurrenceNote: Here “us” refers to Elihu, Job, and his three friends. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-exclusive]])

GLQuote: I am considered to be a liar
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “God considers me to be a liar” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: My wound is incurable
OccurrenceNote: Here Job’s sickness and suffering is spoken of as if it were a “wound.” Alternate translation: “I am sick and no one can heal me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: What man is like Job
OccurrenceNote: Elihu uses this rhetorical question to scold Job. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “There is no one else like Job” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: who drinks up mockery like water
OccurrenceNote: Elihu is accusing Job of mocking others as often as a person drinks water. Alternate translation: “who mocks other people as frequently as he drinks water” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: who walks with wicked men
OccurrenceNote: Here “walk” is an idiom for how a person acts. Alternate translation: “who behaves like wicked men” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: you men of understanding
OccurrenceNote: Elihu is criticizing Job and his friends. He does not actually think they are wise. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-irony]])

GLQuote: far be it from God … far be it from the Almighty that he should commit sin
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases have the same meaning and are used together to emphasize that God would never do anything wrong. The phrase “far be it from” is an idiom. Alternate translation: “Almighty God would never consider doing anything that is wicked or wrong” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: For he pays back a person’s work
OccurrenceNote: This means that he gives to a person what he deserves for the work he has done. Here “work” is a metaphor for what a person does. Alternate translation: “For he gives to a person what he deserves in return for he does” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: he makes every man come upon the reward of his own ways
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “his own ways” is an idiom for how a person lives his life. Elihu emphasizes that God gives to people what they deserve. Alternate translation: “he causes every man to receive the reward he deserves for how he lives” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Who put him in charge over the earth? Who put the whole world under him?
OccurrenceNote: Both of these rhetorical questions have the same meaning and emphasize that no one needed to grant God authority because it was already his. These questions can be written as statements. Alternate translation: “No one needed to give permission to God to take responsibility over all the earth. He is the rightful one to rule the world.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: If he ever
OccurrenceNote: Elihu is describing a situation that he does not believe would ever happen. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hypo]])

GLQuote: his spirit and his breath
OccurrenceNote: The “spirit” and “breath” of God are what makes all living things alive. Alternate translation: “his spirit and breath which give us life” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: all flesh
OccurrenceNote: Here all living things are represented by their “flesh.” Alternate translation: “all living things” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: mankind would return to dust again
OccurrenceNote: This means that all people would die and their bodies would decay and become soil. In the beginning God created man from the dust. Alternate translation: “the bodies of mankind would soon become soil again” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: you have
OccurrenceNote: Here “you” is singular and refers to Job. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-you]])

GLQuote: listen to the sound of my words
OccurrenceNote: “listen to what I say.” This means the same as the previous part of the sentence. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Can one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn God, who is righteous and mighty?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu uses this question to rebuke Job for implying that God hates justice. Alternate translation: “One who hates justice cannot be expected to rule over people. So you really cannot criticize God, who is righteous and powerful, and you cannot say that what he has done is wrong.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Can one who hates justice govern?
OccurrenceNote: The implicit answer to this rhetorical question is “no.” This question implies that God could not rule the world if he hated justice. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “One who hates justice cannot govern the world.” or “God could certainly never hate what is right and still rule the world.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Will you condemn God, who is righteous and mighty?
OccurrenceNote: This rhetorical question is used to emphasize that Job does not have the authority or a reason to condemn God. Alternate translation: “You cannot condemn God, who is righteous and mighty!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: God, who says to a king, ‘You are vile,’ or says to nobles, ‘You are wicked’?
OccurrenceNote: This continues the rhetorical question from the previous verse, emphasizing to Job that he cannot condemn God. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “He says to some kings, ‘You are vile,’ and he says to some nobles, ‘You are wicked.’” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: God, who says to a king
OccurrenceNote: This is part of the previous question. The understood words from the previous verse, “will you condemn God,” may be supplied. Alternate translation: “Will you condemn God, who says to a king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: for they all are the work of his hands
OccurrenceNote: Here “hands” refer to power. Alternate translation: “for God made them all” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: at midnight
OccurrenceNote: Midnight is the time when one day ends and another begins. Here “midnight” is used as an idiom. Alternate translation: “at night” or “suddenly, at night” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: people will be shaken and will pass away
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The phrase “will be shaken” is an idiom that means to be “struck.” Alternate translation: “God strikes them and they die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: mighty people will be taken away, but not by human hands
OccurrenceNote: This means that it is God who causes people to die, not people. Also, If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “it is God and not humans who cause mighty people to die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: not by human hands
OccurrenceNote: Here people are represented by their “hands.” Alternate translation: “not by humans” or “not by people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: For God’s eyes are upon a person’s ways
OccurrenceNote: God’s “eyes” represent his sight. The phrase “a person’s ways” is an idiom for what he does and how he lives. Alternate translation: “For God watches everything a person does” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: he sees all his steps
OccurrenceNote: This means that he always knows where the person is and where he is going. Alternate translation: “he sees him wherever he goes” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: no darkness, no thick gloom
OccurrenceNote: The words “thick gloom” mean basically the same thing as, and intensify, the word “darkness.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: He breaks mighty men into pieces
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of God destroying these men as if he actually broke their bodies into pieces. Alternate translation: “He destroys mighty men” or “He destroys important people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: for their ways that need no further investigation
OccurrenceNote: He does not need to investigate what they have done because he already knows everything about them. Alternate translation: “without needing to do further investigation, because he already knows their ways” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: he puts others in their places
OccurrenceNote: This means that he appoints other people to rule in their positions. Alternate translation: “and he chooses other people to rule in their places” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: in the night
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “when they are not expecting it” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: they are destroyed
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “and destroys them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: In the open sight of others, he kills them for their wicked deeds like criminals
OccurrenceNote: This phrase compares the way that these people die to how criminals die. Alternate translation: “He kills them for their wicked deeds, in the open sight of others as if they were criminals” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: In the open sight of others
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “In a place where everyone can see” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: he kills them
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of God causing these people to die, though he does not actually strike them with a sword himself. He may cause someone else to kill them or disaster to come upon them. Alternate translation: “he causes them to die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: his ways
OccurrenceNote: This refers to God’s instructions for how people should behave. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: they made the cry of poor people come to him
OccurrenceNote: The word “cry” can be expressed as a verb. This speaks of God hearing their cry as if the cry were a person that came to him. Alternate translation: “they made the poor people cry, and God heard them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: When he stays silent, who can condemn him? If he hides his face, who can perceive him?
OccurrenceNote: These two questions speak of God not punishing wicked people as if he were being silent and hiding his face. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: When he stays silent, who can condemn him?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu uses this rhetorical question to teach Job. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “No one can criticize God if he decides to remain silent” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: If he hides his face, who can perceive him?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu uses this rhetorical question to teach Job. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “No one can go and see him if he decides to hide his face” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: his face
OccurrenceNote: Here God is represented by his “face.” Alternate translation: “himself” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: no one to entrap people
OccurrenceNote: This compares a godless ruler harming people as if he were a hunter trapping his prey. Alternate translation: “no one to harm the people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: teach me what I cannot see
OccurrenceNote: Here to “see” means to know. Alternate translation: “teach me what I have done wrong that I am not aware of” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Do you think that God will punish that person’s sin, since you dislike what God does?
OccurrenceNote: “Since you dislike what God does, do you think that God should punish this person’s sin?” Elihu uses this rhetorical question to emphasize that he should not think that God will not punish this man. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Even though you do not like what God does, surely even you do not think that God will punish this person” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: that person’s sin
OccurrenceNote: Here punishing the person because of his sin is referred to as punishing the “person’s sin.” Alternate translation: “that person because of his sin” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: If only Job were put on trial in
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “If only we could put Job on trial in” or “If only we could take Job to court so a judge could listen to” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: in the smallest details of his case
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: “to listen to his case thoroughly” or “to hear all of the details of his case” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: he adds rebellion
OccurrenceNote: This refers to rebellion against God. Alternate translation: “he adds rebellion against God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: he claps his hands in mockery in our midst
OccurrenceNote: In this accusation, this means that Job clapped his hands to strengthen his mockery of God. Alternate translation: “he claps his hands as he mocks God in our midst” or “he mocks God right in front of us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/translate-symaction]])

GLQuote: he piles up words against God
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of “words” as if they were objects, and of speaking many words as if it were piling those objects one on top of the other. Alternate translation: “he speaks many words against God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Do you think this is just…‘My right before God’?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu uses questions to challenge Job. Alternate translation: “You must think you are right…‘My right before God.’” or “It is not just…‘My right before God.’” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Do you think
OccurrenceNote: Here “you” is singular and refers to Job. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-you]])

GLQuote: For you ask, ‘What use is it to me?’ and, ‘Would I be better off if I had sinned?’
OccurrenceNote: Elihu quotes Job as saying the these two rhetorical questions. Alternate translation: “For you say, ‘It does not benefit me’ and, ‘I am no better off than if I had sinned.’” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: If you have sinned … what do you do to him?
OccurrenceNote: These two lines share similar meanings. The second line intensifies the meaning of the first line. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: If you have sinned, what harm do you do to God?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu asks this question to emphasize that Job’s sins cannot actually do anything to God. Alternate translation: “If you have sinned, you have not done any harm to God.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: If your transgressions pile up high, what do you do to him?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of “transgressions” as if they were objects, and of committing many transgressions as if it were piling those objects one on top of the other. He asks this question to emphasize that Job does nothing to God by his transgressions. Alternate translation: “If you committed a great many transgressions, you still do nothing to him.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: If you are righteous, what can you give to him? What will he receive from your hand?
OccurrenceNote: The two rhetorical questions mean basically the same thing, that Job’s righteousness adds nothing to God. Alternate translation: “If you are righteous, that does not enable you to give anything to him, and there is nothing that he will receive from your hand.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: receive from your hand
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “hand” represents Job. Alternate translation: “receive from you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: Because of many acts of oppression
OccurrenceNote: The word “oppression” can be translated with a verbal phrase. Alternate translation: “Because of the many things that people do to oppress others” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: they call for help from the arms of mighty men
OccurrenceNote: Here “arms” refers to power or strength. Alternate translation: “they call for someone to deliver them from the power of mighty men” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: who gives songs in the night
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of God enabling people to have hope in troubling circumstances as if he were giving to them songs which they can sing during the night. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: How much less will he answer you … that you are waiting for him!
OccurrenceNote: Since God will not hear the prayers of prideful, evil men, it is even less likely that he will hear Job, who is complaining against him. Alternate translation: “So he certainly will not answer you … that you are waiting for him!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-exclamations]])

GLQuote: his anger does not punish
OccurrenceNote: Here “his anger” is a metonym for “him.” Alternate translation: “he never punishes anyone because he is angry” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: he piles up words without knowledge
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of “words” as if they were objects, and of speaking many words as if it were piling those objects one on top of the other. The word “knowledge” can be translated with a verbal phrase. Alternate translation: “he speaks many words without knowing what he is talking about” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: I will show you some things
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of explaining things to Job as if he were going to show those things to Job. Alternate translation: “I will explain some things to you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I will obtain my knowledge from far off
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of having knowledge of many different subjects as if it were getting his knowledge from far away places. Alternate translation: “I will show you my great knowledge” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: that righteousness belongs to my Maker
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “righteousness” can be translated with an adjective. Alternate translation: “that my Maker is righteous” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: someone who is mature in knowledge is with you
OccurrenceNote: The word “someone” refers to Elihu himself. He speaks of being very knowledgeable as if it were being mature in knowledge. Alternate translation: “I, who am with you, am very knowledgeable” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: he is mighty in strength of understanding
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “mighty in strength” forms a doublet that means “very strong.” Elihu speaks of God understanding everything perfectly as if his understanding were very strong. Alternate translation: “he is very strong in understanding” or “he understands everything completely” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: He does not withdraw his eyes from righteous people
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of God protecting righteous people as if God were watching them with his eyes, and of God ceasing to protect them as if he withdrew his eyes from them. Alternate translation: “He does not stop protecting the righteous people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: sets them on thrones like kings
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of God honoring the righteous people as if God were causing them to sit on thrones like kings do. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: they are lifted up
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of God honoring the righteous people as if he lifted them up to a high place. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “he lifts them up” or “he honors them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: If they are bound in chains
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “they” refers righteous people whom God will discipline if they sin. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “If someone binds them in chains” or “If someone makes them a prisoner” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: trapped in cords of suffering
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of a person being made to suffer as if that person were trapped in ropes that cause suffering. Alternate translation: “someone causes them to suffer” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: their transgressions and their pride
OccurrenceNote: The verb may be supplied from the previous phrase. Alternate translation: “he reveals to them their transgressions and their pride” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: He also opens their ears
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of causing a person to listen as if it were opening that person’s ear. Alternate translation: “He also causes them to listen” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: to his instruction
OccurrenceNote: The noun “instruction” can be translated with a verbal phrase. Alternate translation: “to what he is instructing them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: to turn back from iniquity
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of stopping an action as if it were turning back from it. Alternate translation: “to stop committing iniquity” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: they will spend their days in prosperity, their years in contentment
OccurrenceNote: The words “days” and “years” both refer to the person’s lifetime. Alternate translation: “they will spend their lives in prosperity and contentment” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: they will perish by the sword
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of a person dying violently as if someone had killed them with a sword. Alternate translation: “they will die a violent death” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: who are godless in heart
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “heart” refers to the thoughts and emotions. The phrase may indicate that the person stubbornly refuses to trust God. Alternate translation: “who refuse to trust in God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: store up their anger
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of a person remaining angry as if that person stored up their anger like one would store up treasure. Alternate translation: “are always angry” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: even when God ties them up
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of God disciplining people as if God were tying them up with ropes. Alternate translation: “even when God punishes them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: he opens their ears
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of God causing a person to listen as if God were opening their ears. See how you translated this in [Job 36:10](../36/10.md). Alternate translation: “he causes them to listen” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: into a broad place where there is no hardship
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of living without trouble as if it were being in a wide-open space where there were no hardships. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: where your table would be set with food full of fatness
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of living prosperously as if it were having one’s table filled with the best foods. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: your table would be set
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “your servants would set your table” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: food full of fatness
OccurrenceNote: Meat that had plenty of fat on it was a sign of prosperity because the animals were healthy and well-fed. Alternate translation: “the very best food” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: judgment and justice have laid hold of you
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of God judging Job and giving him justice as if judgment and justice were people that have laid hold of Job. Alternate translation: “God has brought you to judgment and given you justice” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: Can your wealth benefit you, so that you will not be in distress, or can all the force of your strength help you?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu asks these questions to state that money and power will not be able to help Job if he acts unjustly. Alternate translation: “Your wealth cannot cause you to no longer be in distress, and all the force of your strength cannot help you.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: when peoples are cut off in their place
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) that “peoples” refers to people in general and “cut off in their place” is a metaphor for oppressing others by dragging them away from their homes. Alternate translation: “when people drag others away from their homes” or (2) that “peoples” represents nations and “cut off in their place” is a metaphor for nations being destroyed. Alternate translation: “when nations will perish” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: you are being tested by suffering
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “God is testing you by making you suffer” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: who is a teacher like him?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu asks this rhetorical question to emphasize that no one is a teacher like God. Alternate translation: “no one is a teacher like him.” or “no one teaches like he does.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Who has ever instructed him about his way?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu asks this rhetorical question to emphasize that no one has ever taught God what to do. Alternate translation: “No one has ever instructed him about what he should do.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Who can ever say to him, ‘You have committed unrighteousness?’
OccurrenceNote: Elihu asks this rhetorical question to emphasize that no one can accuse God of having committed unrighteousness. Alternate translation: “No one can ever say to him, ‘You have committed unrighteousness.’” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: they see those deeds only from far away
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of people not being fully able to understand God’s deeds as if people were only able to see those deeds from far away. Alternate translation: “they do not fully understand them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the number of his years is incalculable
OccurrenceNote: This refers to how long God has existed. Alternate translation: “people cannot know how long he has lived” or “people cannot know his age” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: that he distills as rain from his vapor
OccurrenceNote: The word “distills” can also mean “refine” or “filter.” Elihu describes how God turns the drops of water, or vapor, that he draws up into rain. Alternate translation: “that he turns into rain” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: can anyone understand the extensive spread of the clouds and the thunder from his hut?
OccurrenceNote: Elihu asks this rhetorical question to emphasize that no one can do these things. Alternate translation: “no one can understand the extensive spread of the clouds and the thunder from his hut.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: the extensive spread of the clouds
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “the extensive spread” can be translated with a verbal phrase. Alternate translation: “how the clouds spread across the sky” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: from his hut
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of the sky as if it were a “hut” in which God lives. Alternate translation: “from the sky, where God lives” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: and covers the roots of the sea
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of the deep parts of the sea as if the sea were a plant and its depths were its roots. This could mean: (1) although the lightning causes light in the sky, the deep parts of the sea remain dark. Alternate translation: “but the depths of the sea remain dark” or (2) the lightning in the sky cause even the depths of the sea to have light. Alternate translation: “and lights up the depths of the sea” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: He fills his hands with the lightning
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of the lightning that storms cause as if God were holding the lightning in his hand and directing it to strike where he wills. This could mean: (1) that God holds the lightning bolts in his hands in order to throw them, or (2) that God hides the lightning bolts in his hands until he is ready to use them. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: my heart trembles … it is moved out of its place
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize the intensity of his fear. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: it is moved out of its place
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of his heart beating violently as if it were to jump out of his chest. Alternate translation: “it moves out of its place” or “it beats violently” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the noise of his voice, the sound that goes out from his mouth
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Elihu speaks of the thunder as if it is God’s voice. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: to the edges of the earth
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of the farthest places on the earth as if they were the earth’s borders. Alternate translation: “everywhere in the world” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: A voice roars after it … the voice of his majesty
OccurrenceNote: Elihu continues to speak of the thunder as if it is God’s voice. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: when his voice is heard
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “when people hear his voice” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: likewise to the rain shower
OccurrenceNote: The verb may be supplied from the previous phrase. Alternate translation: “likewise, he says to the rain shower” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: He stops the hand of every man
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “hand” represents the entire person. Alternate translation: “He stops every man” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: The storm comes from its chamber in the south and the cold from the scattering winds in the north
OccurrenceNote: In Israel, strong wind storms blow in from the south and cold weather approaches from the north. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: The storm comes from its chamber in the south
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of the storm blowing in from the south as if the storm has a place where it resides until it comes. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: By the breath of God ice is given
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of the cold north wind as if it were God’s breath. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “God’s breath makes ice” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: frozen like metal
OccurrenceNote: Elihu compares the hardness of ice to the hardness of metal. Alternate translation: “frozen, as hard as metal” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: he weighs down the thick cloud with moisture
OccurrenceNote: Elihu speaks of God causing the storm clouds to be full of water as if the moisture weighed heavily on the clouds. Alternate translation: “he causes the thick clouds to be full of moisture” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: sometimes it happens for correction
OccurrenceNote: The word “correction” can be translated with a verbal phrase. The object of his “correction” is people. Alternate translation: “sometimes it happens to correct his people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: sometimes for his land
OccurrenceNote: This means that the rain waters the ground and causes vegetation to grow. Alternate translation: “sometimes to water the land” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])
