OccurrenceNote: These two phrases share similar meanings and are combined for emphasis. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: held my eyes open
OccurrenceNote: Open eyes is a metonym for being unable to sleep. Alternate translation: “kept me from sleeping” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the days of old, about times long past
OccurrenceNote: If necessary, “days of old” and “times long past” can be combined. Alternate translation: “about things that happened a very long time ago” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: I called to mind
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom for remembering. Alternate translation: “I remembered” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Will the Lord reject me forever? Will he never again show me favor?
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases express feeling rejection from the Lord. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: Was his covenant faithfulness gone forever?
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of Yahweh no longer acting faithfully to his covenant as if Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness had gone away. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea with an adjective. Alternate translation: “Has he stopped being faithful to his covenant forever?” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: Had God forgotten to be gracious? Had his anger shut off his compassion?
OccurrenceNote: These are two expressions stating similar concept of God not showing compassion. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: Had his anger shut off his compassion
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of anger as if it were a person shutting a door to keep another person, compassion, from coming out, Alternate translation: “Had God stopped showing us compassion because he was angry with us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: the changing of the right hand of the Most High toward us
OccurrenceNote: The “right hand” is a metonym for power, authority or strength. Alternate translation: “the Most High no longer uses his power to help us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: call to mind
OccurrenceNote: “remember” See how this is translated in [Psalms 74:2](../074/002.md). (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: I will ponder all your deeds and will reflect on them.
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases express the concept of meditating on what Yahweh has done. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: what god compares to our great God?
OccurrenceNote: If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “no god compares to our great God.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: revealed your strength among the peoples
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **strength**, you could express the same idea with an adjective. Alternate translation: “shown people from many people groups how strong you are” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: gave your people victory
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **victory**, you could express the same idea with an adjective. Alternate translation: “caused your people to be victorious” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: The waters saw you … they were afraid … the depths trembled
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of the water as if it were a person who saw something that terrified him. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: the waters saw you, and they were afraid; the depths trembled
OccurrenceNote: “water” and “depth” refers to large bodies of water such as the sea or ocean. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: The clouds poured down water
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of the clouds as if they were people pouring water out of containers. Alternate translation: “Much rain fell” or “It rained very hard” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: your arrows flew about
OccurrenceNote: This is a metaphor that describes lightning as God’s arrows. Alternate translation: “the lightning you made flashed like arrows” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: thunderous voice
OccurrenceNote: This is personification, referring to the thunder as the voice of God. Alternate translation: “voice, which was as loud as thunder” or “very loud voice” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: lightning lit up the world
OccurrenceNote: This is an exaggeration to emphasize that the lightning lit up everything the writer could see. Alternate translation: “lightning lit up everything as far as you could see” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: Your path … your way
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases have similar meanings and are combined for emphasis. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: your footprints
OccurrenceNote: Asaph is speaking of Yahweh as if Yahweh was a person with feet. While this is personification, it should be translated literally, if possible. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: your footprints were not seen
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “no one saw your footprints” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: You led your people like a flock
OccurrenceNote: This simile compares God’s people to a flock of animals. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: hand
OccurrenceNote: Here “hand” is synechdoche for the whole person. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: Hear my teaching
OccurrenceNote: The noun “teaching” can be translated with a verb. Alternate translation: “Hear what I teach” or “Hear me as I teach you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: the words of my mouth
OccurrenceNote: The word “mouth” represents the person. Alternate translation: “my words” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: open my mouth in parables
OccurrenceNote: The idiom “open my mouth” means to speak. Alternate translation: “speak in parables” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: were armed with bows
OccurrenceNote: The soldiers probably also had arrows. Alternate translation: “had bows and arrows for weapons” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: enough to fill the depths of the sea
OccurrenceNote: This is probably hyperbole. Alternate translation: “more water than they could possibly drink” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: Can God really lay out a table for us in the wilderness?
OccurrenceNote: If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “We do not believe that God can really lay out a table for us in the wilderness!” or “God, prove to us that you can really lay out a table for us in the wilderness!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: lay out a table
OccurrenceNote: The idiom “lay out a table” means to prepare a table for a meal. Here the word “table” is a metonym for the food on the table. Alternate translation: “provide us with food” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: But can he give bread also? Will he provide meat for his people?
OccurrenceNote: The people are laughing at God to insult him with these questions. Alternate translation: “But we will not believe that he can give us bread also or provide meat for his people until we see him do it.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: bread … meat
OccurrenceNote: food from plants or food from animals. Though this is a merism for all kinds of food, it is best to translate it literally if possible. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: his fire burned against Jacob
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of Yahweh’s anger as if it were a fire, and of Yahweh acting in anger against Jacob as if that fire burned Jacob. Alternate translation: “his anger was like a fire that burned Jacob” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: his anger attacked Israel
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of Yahweh punishing Israel when he was angry as if his anger were a person who attacked Israel. Alternate translation: “because he was angry, he attacked Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: he commanded the skies
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of the skies as if they were a person who could hear and obey God’s commands. Alternate translation: “he spoke to the sky” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: opened the doors of the sky
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of the sky as if it were a storeroom with doors. Alternate translation: “opened the sky as if it were a storeroom” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the bread of angels
OccurrenceNote: This refers to the manna that God provided for the people. The word “bread” represents food in general. Alternate translation: “the same kind of food that angels eat” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: food in abundance
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **abundance**, you could express the same idea with an adjective. Alternate translation: “abundant food” or “a large amount of food” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: He rained down meat on them like dust
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of Yahweh causing birds to fall from the sky as if the birds were rain that Yahweh caused to fall. He compares the large amount of birds to dust. Alternate translation: “He caused meat to fall from the sky like rain, and there was so much of it that it covered the ground like dust” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: as numerous as the sands of the sea
OccurrenceNote: No one can count the grains of sand. There were more birds than anyone could count, but this is an exaggeration: there were probably not literally the same number of birds as grains of sand. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: God’s anger attacked them
OccurrenceNote: “God was angry and attacked them.” See how “his anger attacked Israel” is translated in [Psalms 78:21](../078/021.md). (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: brought down
OccurrenceNote: This is a euphemism that means he caused them to die. Alternate translation: “killed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: did not believe his wonderful deeds
OccurrenceNote: The word “deeds” is a metonym for God, who did the deeds. What they did not believe can be stated clearly. Alternate translation: “did not believe that he would take care of them even though he had done such wonderful deeds” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: cut short their days
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “days” refers to a lifetime. The idiom “to cut short … days” means to cause someone to die before they have lived a long life. Alternate translation: “killed them while they were still young” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]])

GLQuote: their years were filled with terror
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of years as if they were containers. Alternate translation: “year after year they were afraid all the time” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: to seek him
OccurrenceNote: to ask him what they needed to do so he would protect them (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: God was their rock
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks about God as if he were a hill or mountain where people could go to be safe from their enemies. Alternate translation: “God was the one who protected them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: with their mouth
OccurrenceNote: The word “mouth” is a metonym for the words they spoke using their mouths. Alternate translation: “by saying what they said” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: their hearts were not firmly fixed on him
OccurrenceNote: Here “hearts” is a metonym for their thoughts. To be loyal to him is spoken of as being solidly attached to him. Alternate translation: “their thoughts were not focused on him” or “they were not loyal to him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: held back his anger
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of God’s anger as if it were an angry person whom God held onto to keep him from attacking the one who had made him angry. Alternate translation: “did not punish them even though he was angry with them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: did not stir up all his wrath
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of God’s wrath as if it were a sleeping person whom God allowed to sleep and did not awaken. Alternate translation: “did not allow himself to become fully angry with them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: called to mind
OccurrenceNote: “remembered.” See how “call to mind” is translated in [Psalms 20:3](../020/003.md). (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: they were made of flesh
OccurrenceNote: The word “flesh,” which is weak and then dies, is a metonym for human weakness and death. Alternate translation: “the Israelites were weak and would someday die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: that devoured them
OccurrenceNote: The flies made the Egyptians almost as unhappy as they would have if they had eaten the Egyptians. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: He gave their crops to the grasshopper
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of the crops as a gift that God gave to the grasshoppers. Alternate translation: “He allowed the grasshopper to eat their crops” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: their labor to the locust
OccurrenceNote: “he gave their labor to the locust.” Asaph speaks of the people’s labor as if it were a gift that God gave to the grasshoppers. The word “labor” is a metonym for the crops that their labor had produced. Alternate translation: “he allowed the locusts to eat the crops they had worked so hard to produce” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: The fierceness of his anger lashed out against them
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of God’s fierceness as if it were a person who could attack another person. Alternate translation: “He was angry with them, so he suddenly and fiercely attacked them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: He sent wrath, fury, and trouble like agents who bring disaster
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of wrath, fury, and trouble as though they are people God can send to do his work for him. Alternate translation: “He was so angry that he wanted to harm the Egyptians, so he made trouble for them and brought them to disaster” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: He leveled a path for his anger
OccurrenceNote: The psalmist speaks of anger as if it were a person who could walk Yahweh getting ready to punish the people as if he were making a smooth road for a person to walk on. Alternate translation: “He was so angry that he did everything he could to harm them” or “It was as if his anger was an army and he made a smooth road for it to march on” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: gave them over to the plague
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of the plague as if it were a person who was going to harm the Egyptians. Alternate translation: “he made them all very ill with the plague” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: the firstborn of their strength
OccurrenceNote: This phrase refers to the firstborn males of each family. Alternate translation: “the firstborn males” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: in the tents of Ham
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “tents” is a metonym for families. The word “Ham” refers to Egypt by the name of their ancestor. Alternate translation: “among the families of Egypt” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: like sheep … like a flock
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks about the Israelites as if they were sheep. This means God cared for and protected the people like a shepherd does his sheep. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: his right hand acquired
OccurrenceNote: The words “right hand” are a metonym for power. Alternate translation: “he won for himself using his own power” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: in their tents
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) he settled Israel in their own tents in the land or (2) he settled Israel in the tents from which he had driven the other nations. Most of these “tents” were actually houses, both when the other nations lived in them and when the Israelites lived in them. Alternate translation: “in their homes” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: challenged and defied
OccurrenceNote: These words mean almost the same thing. The writer uses them both to emphasize that the Israelites did not believe that God would either provide for them or punish evil as he had said he would. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: were unfaithful and acted treacherously
OccurrenceNote: These words mean almost the same thing. The writer uses them both to emphasize that the Israelites did not do for God what they had said they would do. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-doublet]])

GLQuote: made him angry with their high places and provoked him to jealous anger with their idols
OccurrenceNote: These two phrases are in parallel and have similar meanings. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: He allowed his strength to be captured and gave his glory into the enemy’s hand
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of God’s strength and glory as if they were physical objects that people could capture and hold. The words “strength” and “glory” are probably mentonyms for the ark of the covenant. The word “hand” is a metonym for the enemy’s power. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “He allowed his enemies to capture the glorious ark of his covenant; he simply gave it to them so they could do whatever they wanted with it” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: He handed his people over to the sword
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of God’s people as if they were a small object God would give as a gift, and of the sword, a metonym for death in war, as if it were a person who could receive a gift. Alternate translation: “He allowed people to kill all his people in war” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Fire devoured their young men
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) “The enemy used fire to kill all their young men” or (2) “Their young men died quickly in battle like a fire burns dry grass.” Do not communicate that these people used guns. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Their priests fell by the sword
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “sword” represents soldiers who fought with swords. The phrase “fell by the sword” is an idiom that means to die in battle. Alternate translation: “Their priests died in battle” or “Enemies killed their priests with swords” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: the Lord awakened as one from sleep
OccurrenceNote: The Lord not acting for a period of time is spoken of as if he were asleep, and his beginning to act is spoken of as if he awakened. Alternate translation: “the Lord began to act as if he had awakened from sleep” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the tent of Joseph
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “tent” is a metonym for a family. In this phrase it refers to the descendants of Joseph. Alternate translation: “the descendants of Joseph” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: He built his sanctuary like the heavens
OccurrenceNote: This simile could mean: (1) Yahweh has made his sanctuary as high as the heavens. Alternate translation: “He built his sanctuary high, like the heavens” or (2) Yahweh has made his sanctuary as permanent as the heavens. Alternate translation: “He built his sanctuary to last permanently, like the heavens last forever” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: like the earth
OccurrenceNote: The verb may be supplied from the previous line. The writer compares the permanence of Yahweh’s sanctuary to the permanence of the earth. Alternate translation: “He built his sanctuary to last permanently, like the earth lasts permanently” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: from the sheepfolds
OccurrenceNote: “from where he was working in the sheepfolds” [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]]

GLQuote: to be shepherd of Jacob, his people, and of Israel, his heritage
OccurrenceNote: The word “shepherd” is a metaphor for one who leads and protects other people. Alternate translation: “to lead and protect the descendants of Jacob, his people, and of Israel, his heritage” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: David shepherded them
OccurrenceNote: The word “shepherded” is a metaphor for leading and protecting. Alternate translation: “David led them and protected them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: They have shed their blood like water
OccurrenceNote: The word “blood” is a metonym for innocent life. To shed blood is to kill innocent people. Most people saw water every day, so for blood to be as common as water, many innocent people would have to die. Alternate translation: “They have killed so many innocent people that the blood is everywhere, like water after it rains” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: We have become a reproach for our neighbors, mocking and derision to those who are around us
OccurrenceNote: The words “reproach,” “mocking,” and “derision” are metonyms for those whom others reproach, mock, and deride. Alternate translation: “We have become people whom our neighbors reproach; those around us mock and deride us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: How long will your jealous anger burn like fire?
OccurrenceNote: If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “It seems as though your jealous anger will never stop burning like fire.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: will your jealous anger burn
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **anger**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form such as “angry.” Alternate translation: “will you be jealous and angry” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: burn like fire
OccurrenceNote: This simile compares the expression of God’s anger to a fire that destroys things. Alternate translation: “destroy us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: General Information:
OccurrenceNote: These two pairs of phrases each share similar meanings and are combined for emphasis. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Pour out your wrath on the nations
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of God’s wrath as if it were a liquid. Alternate translation: “Since you are angry, punish the nations” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: do not call upon your name
OccurrenceNote: The word “name” is a metonym for the person’s power and authority. Alternate translation: “do not belong to you” or “do not ask you to help them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: they have devoured Jacob
OccurrenceNote: The word “Jacob” is a mentonym for his descendants, the people of Israel. Alternate translation: “they have completely destroyed the people of Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: we are very low
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of the people being weak and discouraged as if they were in a low position. Alternate translation: “we are very weak” or “we are very discouraged” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: God of our salvation
OccurrenceNote: The word “salvation” can be translated with the verb “save”: “God who saves us.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: for the sake of the glory of your name
OccurrenceNote: The word “name” is a metonym for his reputation, for what people know about him. Alternate translation: “so that people will know about your glory” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: for your name’s sake
OccurrenceNote: God’s name here represents his whole being and the honor that he deserves. Alternate translation: “so that people will honor you” or “for your own sake” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Why should the nations say, “Where is their God?”
OccurrenceNote: If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “The nations should not be able to say, ‘Where is their God?’” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Where is their God?
OccurrenceNote: This taunt can be translated as a statement. Alternate translation: “Their God cannot do anything!” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: May the blood of your servants that was shed be avenged on the nations before our eyes
OccurrenceNote: To shed blood is a metonym for killing innocent people. This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “Avenge your innocent servants whom the nations killed where we can see you do it” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: May the groans of the prisoners come before you
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of the sound made by prisoners in pain and sorrow as if it were a person who appears before a king. Alternate translation: “Listen carefully to the groans of the prisoners and help them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: children of death
OccurrenceNote: This is an idiom that refers to people who are condemned to death. Alternate translation: “those who are condemned to die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Pay back … the insults … Lord
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of the evil deeds that the neighboring countries did against Israel as “insults,” and as if they were physical items. He asks the Lord to count those deeds, and for every one that the neighboring countries committed, he asks the Lord to have someone do seven evil deeds to the neighboring countries. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: into the laps
OccurrenceNote: onto their knees and thighs as they are sitting. This is a metaphor for “directly and personally.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: we your people and sheep of your pasture will give you thanks
OccurrenceNote: The word “sheep” is a metaphor for helpless people whom a shepherd protects and leads. Alternate translation: “we who are your people, whom you protect and lead, will thank you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: your praises
OccurrenceNote: This represents the things that people will praise them the Lord for. Alternate translation: “continue to praise you for the things that you have done” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Shepherd of Israel
OccurrenceNote: Asaph is referring to God as the one who leads and protects Israel. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: you who lead Joseph like a flock
OccurrenceNote: The word “Joseph” refers to the nation of Israel. Asaph speaks of the people as if they were a flock of sheep that Yahweh, who is the shepherd, leads. Alternate translation: “you who lead the descendants of Joseph as though they were a flock of sheep” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Joseph
OccurrenceNote: Here Joseph represents the nation of Israel. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: you who sit above the cherubim
OccurrenceNote: You may need to make explicit that the cherubim are those on the lid of the ark of the covenant. The biblical writers often spoke of the ark of the covenant as if it were Yahweh’s footstool upon which he rested his feet as he sat on his throne in heaven above. Alternate translation: “you who sit on your throne above the cherubim on the ark of the covenant” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: shine on us
OccurrenceNote: Asaph speaks of God as if he were the sun, giving light, a metaphor for moral goodness. Alternate translation: “give us light” or “show us the right way to live” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: stir up your power
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “stir up” means to “put into action.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: make your face shine on us
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of Yahweh acting favorably towards them as if Yahweh’s face shone a light on them. Alternate translation: “act favorably towards us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: and we will be saved
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated in active form. Alternate translation: “and please save us” or “so that you can save us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: You have fed them with the bread of tears and given them tears to drink in great quantities
OccurrenceNote: The words “bread of tears” and “tears to drink” are metaphors for continual sadness. Alternate translation: “You have made sure that they are very sad all the time” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: make your face shine on us
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of Yahweh acting favorably towards them as if Yahweh’s face shone a light on them. See how you translated this in [Psalms 80:3](../080/003.md). Alternate translation: “act favorably towards us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: we will be saved
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “you will save us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: You brought a vine out of Egypt
OccurrenceNote: Asaph compares the nation of Israel to a vine made ready to transplant. Alternate translation: “You brought us, like a vine, out of Egypt” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: you drove out nations and transplanted it
OccurrenceNote: The psalmist speaks of his people as if they were a plant that Yahweh was transplanting. Alternate translation: “you drove out nations from their land and gave it to us, the vine, and planted us there” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: The mountains were covered with its shade, the cedars of God by its branches
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Its shade covered the mountains, its branches the cedars of God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the cedars of God by its branches
OccurrenceNote: “and the cedars of God were covered by its branches,” which copies the verb from the previous sentence. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “and its branches covered the cedars of God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Turn back
OccurrenceNote: The writer wants God to turn back in order to help them. This can be stated explicitly. Alternate translation: “Turn back to us” or “Come and help us again” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: this vine
OccurrenceNote: The writer continues comparing the nation of Israel to the vine. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: This is the root that your right hand planted
OccurrenceNote: The right hand represents the Yahweh’s power and control. Alternate translation: “This is the root that you, Yahweh, planted” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: your hand
OccurrenceNote: This refers to Yahweh’s power and control. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the man of your right hand
OccurrenceNote: the nation of Israel, which Yahweh has chosen as his people. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: right hand
OccurrenceNote: When a man in Israel wanted to honor another man, he would have that other man stand at his right side, close to his right hand. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: we will not turn away from you
OccurrenceNote: Here “turn away” is a metaphor for rejecting someone. This can also be stated in positive form. Alternate translation: “we will not stop worshiping and obeying you” or “we will always worship and obey you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: shine on us
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of Yahweh acting favorably towards them as if Yahweh’s face shone a light on them. See how you translated this in [Psalms 80:3](../080/003.md). Alternate translation: “act favorably towards us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: we will be saved
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “you will save us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: God our strength
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **strength**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form such as “strong.” Alternate translation: “God who causes us to be strong” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: the God of Jacob
OccurrenceNote: Here “Jacob” represents all of his descendants. Alternate translation: “the God of Israel, the nation of Jacob’s descendants” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: a decree given by the God of Jacob
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “the God of Jacob decreed it” or “the God of Jacob commanded it” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the God of Jacob
OccurrenceNote: Here “Jacob” represents all of his descendants. Alternate translation: “the God of Israel, the nation of Jacob’s descendants” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: in Joseph
OccurrenceNote: Here “Joseph” represents all of the Israelites. Alternate translation: “to the Israelites” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: when he went against the land of Egypt
OccurrenceNote: This refers to the historical events in Egypt when the people of Israel were enslaved and God rescued them. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: the land of Egypt
OccurrenceNote: Here “land” represents the people. Alternate translation: “the people of Egypt” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: removed the burden from his shoulder
OccurrenceNote: Here “the burden from his shoulder” represents the forced labor the Israelites had to do as slaves in Egypt. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: his hands were freed from holding the basket
OccurrenceNote: Here “holding the basket” represents the forced labor the Israelites had to do as slaves in Egypt. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: I answered you from a dark thundercloud
OccurrenceNote: When God came to the Israelites, he hid the fullness of his presence and glory in a dark and threatening cloud. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: I tested you at the waters of Meribah
OccurrenceNote: God tested the children of Israel to see if they would trust him to supply water in the desert of Meribah. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Israel
OccurrenceNote: Here “Israel” represents the people of Israel. Alternate translation: “Israelites” or “people of Israel” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it
OccurrenceNote: God taking care of all the needs of the people is spoken of as if he were a mother bird feeding her baby birds. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: So I gave them over to their own stubborn way
OccurrenceNote: God allowing the people to remain stubborn is spoken of as if God were giving them over to an enemy to let the enemy harm them. Alternate translation: “Therefore, I let them be stubborn” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: oh, that my people would walk in my paths
OccurrenceNote: God wanting the people to obey him is spoken of as if he wanted the people to walk on his paths or roads. Alternate translation: “I wish that they would obey my laws” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: turn my hand against
OccurrenceNote: Here “hand” represents Yahweh’s power. Alternate translation: “I would destroy” or “I would defeat” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: who hate Yahweh … before him
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh is speaking about himself in the third person. Alternate translation: “who hate me … before me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: May they be humiliated forever
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “I would humiliate them forever” or “I will punish them forever” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: I would feed Israel with the finest wheat
OccurrenceNote: God causing the best wheat to grow in Israel is spoken of as if he would literally feed the wheat to the people. Alternate translation: “I would allow the Israelites to eat the finest wheat” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: honey out of the rock
OccurrenceNote: This refers to wild honey. Bees would build hives in the holes in rocks and make the honey there. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: he renders judgment
OccurrenceNote: “he gives judgment.” If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **judgment**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form. Alternate translation: “he judges” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: How long will you judge unjustly and show favoritism to the wicked?
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh uses a question to rebuke the gods for not judging people fairly. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: poor … fatherless … afflicted … destitute
OccurrenceNote: These words are nominal adjectives. They can be stated as adjectives. Alternate translation: “those who are poor … those who are fatherless … those who are afflicted … those who are destitute” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]])

GLQuote: poor … needy … wicked
OccurrenceNote: These are all nominal adjectives. They can be stated as adjectives. Alternate translation: “those who are poor … those who are needy … those who are wicked” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]])

GLQuote: take them out of the hand of the wicked
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “hand” represents power or control. Alternate translation: “stop the wicked people from harming them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: they wander around in the darkness
OccurrenceNote: Doing what is evil is spoken of as if they were walking in a very dark place. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: all the foundations of the earth crumble
OccurrenceNote: The gods corrupting the moral order that Yahweh established is spoken of as if the gods were shaking the earth and making it fall apart. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: sons of the Most High
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh is speaking about himself as “the Most High.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: and fall
OccurrenceNote: This is a way of speaking of a person dying. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: judge the earth
OccurrenceNote: Here “earth” represents the people. Alternate translation: “judge the people of the earth” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: for you have an inheritance in all the nations
OccurrenceNote: “for all the nations are your inheritance.” Yahweh taking all the people as his own and ruling over them is spoken of as if the nations were a possession that he inherited. Alternate translation: “for you rule over all the people of every nation” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: all the nations
OccurrenceNote: Here “nations” represents the people of the nations. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: those who hate you have raised their heads
OccurrenceNote: The phrase “raised their heads” is way of saying they are rebelling against God. Alternate translation: “those who hate you are defying you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: the name of Israel will no longer be remembered
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” represents a reputation or the memory of someone. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “no one will ever remember the Israelites existed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: the tents of Edom
OccurrenceNote: This refers to the people of Edom who lived in tents. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Gebal, Ammon, Amalek … Philistia
OccurrenceNote: These all represent the people of each area or tribe. Alternate translation: “the people of Gebal, the Ammonites, the Amalekites … the Philistines” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Assyria
OccurrenceNote: This represents the people of Assyria. Alternate translation: “the people of Assyria” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: they have become an arm for the descendants of Lot
OccurrenceNote: Here “arm” is a metonym that represents “help.” Alternate translation: “they have become a help for the descendants of Lot” or “they are helping the descendants of Lot” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the descendants of Lot
OccurrenceNote: This refers to the people of the nations of Moab and Ammon. You can make clear the understood information. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: Do to them as you did to Midian … Sisera and to Jabin
OccurrenceNote: The writer is asking God to defeat Israel’s enemies as he has done in the past. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: did to Midian
OccurrenceNote: Here “Midian” represents the people of Midian. Alternate translation: “did to the Midianites” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: became like manure for the earth
OccurrenceNote: This means the bodies of Sisera and Jabin were not buried but were left to rot. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: the pastures of God
OccurrenceNote: This speaks about the land of Israel as if it were land for sheep to graze and God were the shepherd watching over it. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: General Information:
OccurrenceNote: The writer uses similes to describe God’s total destruction of Israel’s enemies. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: make them like the whirling dust, like chaff before the wind
OccurrenceNote: Both statements speak of God destroying his enemies as if he were a strong wind easily blowing them away. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: like the fire that burns the forest, and like the flame that sets the mountains on fire
OccurrenceNote: Both statements speak of God’s punishment as if it were a fire, and the enemies of God are things that burn in the fire. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Chase them with your strong wind, and terrify them with your windstorm
OccurrenceNote: Both statements ask God to destroy the enemies with storms. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]])

GLQuote: Fill their faces with shame
OccurrenceNote: Here “faces” represents the whole person. Alternate translation: “Make them very ashamed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: they might seek your name
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” represents God’s power. God’s enemies acknowledging that God is powerful is spoken of as if they are seeking to find Yahweh. Alternate translation: “they might acknowledge that you are powerful” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: May they be put to shame and be terrified forever
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Make them ashamed and terrified forever” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: are the Most High over all the earth
OccurrenceNote: God ruling over everything in the earth is spoken of as if he were elevated higher than everything else. Alternate translation: “are supreme, and you rule all things on the earth” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the courts of Yahweh
OccurrenceNote: Here “courts” represent the temple. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: My heart and all of my being call out
OccurrenceNote: Here “heart” represents the whole person. Alternate translation: “I call out with all of my being” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: the swallow a nest
OccurrenceNote: Here the words “has found” or “has made” are understood. Alternate translation: “the swallow has found a nest” or “the swallow has made a nest” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: Blessed is the man
OccurrenceNote: Here “man” refers to people in general. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-genericnoun]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-gendernotations]])

GLQuote: whose strength is in you
OccurrenceNote: God is spoken of as if strength was actually found in him. Alternate translation: “whom you strengthen” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: in whose heart are the highways up to Zion
OccurrenceNote: This expression is about heart-felt desire. Alternate translation: “Who love to go up to Zion” or “Who earnestly wish go up to Zion” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: blessings
OccurrenceNote: Here the word “blessings” is a metonym for the pools of water that make people who live in dry lands happy. Alternate translation: “pools of water that make them happy” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: They go from strength to strength
OccurrenceNote: This is a way of saying they get stronger. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: God, watch over our shield
OccurrenceNote: The king who protects his people is spoken of as if he were a shield. Alternate translation: “God, watch over our king” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: For one day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere
OccurrenceNote: This can be stated with the understood information. Alternate translation: “I would rather be in your courts for one day than to be somewhere else for a thousand days” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]])

GLQuote: the wicked
OccurrenceNote: This nominal adjective can be stated as an adjective. Alternate translation: “wicked people” or “those who are wicked” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]])

GLQuote: For Yahweh God is our sun and shield
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh who guides and protects his people is spoken of as if he were the sun and a shield. Alternate translation: “For Yahweh God guides us like the light from the sun, and he protects us like a shield” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Yahweh will give grace and glory
OccurrenceNote: The abstract nouns “grace” and “glory” can be stated as verbs. Alternate translation: “Yahweh will be kind to us and honor us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: blessed is the man
OccurrenceNote: Here “man” means people in general. Alternate translation: “blessed are those” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-genericnoun]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-gendernotations]])

GLQuote: you have showed favor to your land
OccurrenceNote: Here “land” represents the nation and people of Israel. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: of Jacob
OccurrenceNote: Here “Jacob” represents Jacob’s descendents, the Israelites. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: you have covered all their sin
OccurrenceNote: Here sin that is forgiven is spoken of as if it were covered so that it can not be seen. Alternate translation: “you have deliberately forgotten their sin” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: You have withdrawn all your wrath
OccurrenceNote: God no longer punishing the Israelites is spoken of as if wrath were an object that Yahweh could take away from the Israelites. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: you have turned back from your hot anger
OccurrenceNote: God no longer being angry with the Israelites is spoken of as if anger were a fire that God from which God turned away. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: God of our salvation
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **salvation**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form. Alternate translation: “God who saves us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: let go of your displeasure with us
OccurrenceNote: Asking God to stop being angry with the Israelites is spoken of as if displeasure were an object the writer wants God to let go of. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Will you be angry with us forever? Will you remain angry throughout future generations?
OccurrenceNote: The writer uses these questions to emphasize that he is requesting God to stop being angry with them. These rhetorical questions can be translated as a statement. Alternate translation: “Please do not stay angry at us forever.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Will you not revive us again?
OccurrenceNote: The writer uses a question to emphasize his request to God to make the people of Israel prosper and happy again. If your readers would misunderstand this question, you can express it as a statement. Alternate translation: “Please make us prosper again.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Show us your covenant faithfulness
OccurrenceNote: If the sentence is rearranged, the ideas in If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea with the phrase “faithful to your covenant.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: grant us your salvation
OccurrenceNote: This is how the writer wants God to show his faithfulness to his people. If the sentence is rearranged, the ideas in If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **salvation**, you could express the same idea with the verb “save.” Alternate translation: “and save us” or “by saving us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: Yet they must not turn again to foolish ways
OccurrenceNote: A person changing the way he behaves is spoken of as if he were physically turning to a different direction. Alternate translation: “Yet they must not start doing foolish things again” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Surely his salvation is near to those
OccurrenceNote: God being ready to save someone is spoken of as if salvation were an object that God has placed near someone. Alternate translation: “Surely God is ready to save those” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: then glory will remain in our land
OccurrenceNote: Here “glory” represents God’s presence. Alternate translation: “then his glorious presence will remain in our land” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Covenant faithfulness and trustworthiness have met together
OccurrenceNote: The abstract nouns “faithfulness” and “trustworthiness” are spoken of as if they were persons who meet together. This could mean: (1) God has been faithful because of his covenant and has done what he promised to do. Alternate translation: “God has been faithful to his covenant and has proven that he is worthy of people trusting him” or (2) God has been faithful because of his covenant and the people have responded by being faithful to him. Alternate translation: “God has been faithful to his covenant and people have responded by trusting him” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: righteousness and peace have kissed each other
OccurrenceNote: This could mean: (1) the people will do what is right and God will cause the people to live in peace or (2) God will do what is right and will cause the people to live in peace. Either way righteousness and peace are abstract nouns and are spoken of as if they were persons who kiss each other. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: Trustworthiness springs up from the ground
OccurrenceNote: The people on earth being faithful to God is spoken of as if trustworthiness were a plant growing out of the ground. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **trustworthiness**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form such as “loyal.” Alternate translation: “Here on earth, we will be loyal to God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: righteousness looks down from the sky
OccurrenceNote: The word “righteousness” is an abstract noun, and it is spoken of as a person looking down as God does. Alternate translation: “God will look on us from heaven and will act justly towards us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: Righteousness will go before him and make a way for his footsteps
OccurrenceNote: God doing what is right everywhere he goes is spoken of as if righteousness were a person who goes ahead of God and prepares a path for God to walk. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: his footsteps
OccurrenceNote: Here “footsteps” represents where God walks. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: save your servant
OccurrenceNote: David refers to himself as “your servant,” that is, God’s servant. Alternate translation: “save me, your servant” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: all day long
OccurrenceNote: This is an exaggeration. David cries out continually, but not literally at all times from dawn to dusk. Alternate translation: “continually” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: Make your servant glad
OccurrenceNote: David refers to himself as “your servant,” that is, God’s servant. Alternate translation: “Make me, your servant” or “Make me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: among the gods
OccurrenceNote: The writer is not acknowledging these other gods exist. He is referring to false gods that people from other nations worship. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: All the nations
OccurrenceNote: Here “the nations” represent the people. Alternate translation: “The people from all nations” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: They will honor your name
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” represents the whole person. Alternate translation: “They will honor you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Teach me your ways, Yahweh. Then I will walk in your truth
OccurrenceNote: A person who obeys what God wants is spoken of as if he were walking on God’s way or road. Alternate translation: “Teach me your truth, Yahweh. Then I will obey what you say” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Unite my heart to reverence you
OccurrenceNote: Here “heart” represents a person’s thoughts, emotions, and motives. Asking God to cause a person to respect him completely is spoken of as if the person’s heart were in many pieces and that God unites them together. Alternate translation: “Cause me to respect you sincerely with all my heart” or “Cause me to respect you sincerely” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I will praise you with my whole heart
OccurrenceNote: Here “heart” represents a person’s thoughts, emotions, and motives. Alternate translation: “I will praise you completely and sincerely” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I will glorify your name
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” represents the whole person. Alternate translation: “I will glorify you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: For great is your covenant faithfulness toward me
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea with an adjective. Alternate translation: “For you are very faithful to me because of your covenant” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: the arrogant
OccurrenceNote: This nominal adjective can be stated as an adjective. Alternate translation: “arrogant people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]])

GLQuote: seek my life
OccurrenceNote: This is a way of saying they want to kill him. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: and abundant in covenant faithfulness and trustworthiness
OccurrenceNote: God constantly being faithful and trustworthy is spoken of as if faithfulness and trustworthiness were objects of which God has a large quantity. The two abstract nouns can be translated as adjectives. Alternate translation: “always faithful to your covenant and very worthy of people trusting you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: Turn toward me
OccurrenceNote: Asking God to consider him is spoken of as if he wanted God to turn and look at him. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: give your strength to your servant
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **strength**, you could express the same idea with a verb or an adjective. Alternate translation: “strengthen your servant” or “make your servant strong” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: your servant … the son of your servant woman
OccurrenceNote: The writer is speaking about himself in the third person. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]])

GLQuote: be put to shame
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “they will be ashamed” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: gates of Zion
OccurrenceNote: Here “gates of Zion” represents the entire city of Jerusalem. Alternate translation: “city of Jerusalem” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-synecdoche]])

GLQuote: all the tents of Jacob
OccurrenceNote: The people lived in tents while they wandered in the desert. Here the writer uses “tents of Jacob” to represent where the Israelites live now. Alternate translation: “any of the other dwelling places of the Israelites” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: Glorious things are said of you, city of God
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks to the city of Jerusalem as if it were listening to him. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “You people in Jerusalem, other people say wonderful things about your city” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-apostrophe]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Rahab and Babylon
OccurrenceNote: Here “Rahab” is a poetic way of referring to Egypt. Both “Rahab” and “Babylon” represent the people. Alternate translation: “the people of Egypt and Babylon” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/translate-names]])

GLQuote: This one was born there
OccurrenceNote: “This one” refers to the people from the nations that the writer mentions. Although they were not physically born in Zion, those who follow God are natives of Jerusalem spiritually. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Of Zion it will be said
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “People will say about Zion” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: Each of these was born in her
OccurrenceNote: People from other nations that worship Yahweh are spoken of as if they were born in Jerusalem. Alternate translation: “It is as though all of these people were born in Jerusalem” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: the Most High himself
OccurrenceNote: The writer uses the reflexive pronoun “himself” to emphasize that it is the Most High who is doing this. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rpronouns]])

GLQuote: Yahweh writes in the census book of the nations
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh acknowledging that the people from other nations belong to him is spoken of as if he were a king writing down the names of the people who live in his city. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: This one was born there
OccurrenceNote: “This one” refers to the people from the nations that the writer mentions. Although they were not physically born in Zion, those who follow God are natives of Jerusalem spiritually. See how you translated this in [Psalms 87:4](../087/004.md). (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: All my fountains are in you
OccurrenceNote: Jerusalem being a place where people receive all their blessings is spoken of as if Jerusalem were a spring that provided water to the people. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: God of my salvation
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **salvation**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form. Alternate translation: “you are the one who saves me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: day and night
OccurrenceNote: The writer uses these words with opposite meanings to say that he cries out continually. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-merism]])

GLQuote: For I am filled with troubles
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of himself as if he were a container and troubles are the contents that fill the container. Alternate translation: “For I am very troubled” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: my life has reached Sheol
OccurrenceNote: Here “life” represents the writer. And “Sheol” represents death. The writer speaks about himself possibly dying soon as if Sheol were a place and he has arrived at that place. Alternate translation: “I am about to die” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: People treat me like those who go down into the pit
OccurrenceNote: The word “pit” means the same as “Sheol.” The phrase “go down into the pit” represents dying. Alternate translation: “people treat me like I have already died” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: I am abandoned among the dead
OccurrenceNote: People treating the writer as if he were already dead is spoken of as if he were a corpse that they left unburied. Alternate translation: I am left alone as if I were dead” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I am like the dead who lie in the grave
OccurrenceNote: The writer feeling like people and God have abandoned him speaks about himself as if he were already a dead person lying in a grave. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: the dead who lie
OccurrenceNote: The nominal adjective “the dead” can be stated as an adjective. Alternate translation: “a dead person who lies” or “dead people who lie” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-nominaladj]])

GLQuote: they are cut off from your power
OccurrenceNote: God no longer using his power to help dead people is spoken of as if God literally cut him off or removed him from his power. Alternate translation: “you no longer use your power to help them” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: You place me in the lowest part of the pit, in the dark and deep places
OccurrenceNote: The writer feeling like God has abandoned him speaks about himself as if God has put the him in the deepest and darkest grave. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Your wrath lies heavy on me
OccurrenceNote: This speaks about God being very angry with the writer as if God’s wrath were a heavy object lying on top of the writer. Alternate translation: “I feel your great anger” or “I feel how very angry you are with me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: all your waves crash over me
OccurrenceNote: This speaks about God being very angry with the writer as if God’s anger were large waves rising up from the sea then landing on the writer. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I am hemmed in
OccurrenceNote: The writer’s physical condition that makes him repulsive to his friends is spoken of as if he were in closed into a confining space. Alternate translation: “It is as though I were in a prison” or “I am trapped” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: My eyes grow weary from trouble
OccurrenceNote: Here “eyes” represents a person’s ability to see. For his eyes to grow weary from trouble is a way of saying that he his troubles cause him to cry so much that it is hard for him to see. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: Will you do wonders for the dead?
OccurrenceNote: The writer uses a question to emphasize that if God lets him die then God will no longer be able to do wonderful things for him. Alternate translation: “You do not do wonders for dead people.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Will those who have died rise and praise you?
OccurrenceNote: The writer uses a question to emphasize that if God lets him die then he will not be able to praise God any longer. Alternate translation: “You know that those who have died will not stand up and praise you.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Will your covenant faithfulness be proclaimed in the grave, your loyalty in the place of the dead?
OccurrenceNote: Both questions mean the same thing. The writer uses questions to emphasize that a dead person is not able to praise God’s faithfulness. The abstract nouns “faithfulness” and “loyalty” can be translated as adjectives. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “Nobody will proclaim your covenant faithfulness or loyalty from the grave.” or “Nobody will proclaim from the grave that you are faithful to your covenant and loyal to your people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: your loyalty in the place of the dead?
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated as a separate sentence. Alternate translation: “Will your loyalty be proclaimed in the place of the dead?” or “Those who are dead will not proclaim your loyalty.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Will your wonderful deeds be known in the darkness, or your righteousness in the place of forgetfulness?
OccurrenceNote: Both questions mean the same thing. The writer uses questions to emphasize that those who are dead are not able to experience or proclaim the great things God does. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “People will not talk about your wonderful deeds and righteousness in the dark place of the forgotten dead.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: or your righteousness in the place of forgetfulness?
OccurrenceNote: This can be translated as a separate sentence. Alternate translation: “Will your righteousness be known in the place of forgetfulness?” or “Those who are in the place of forgetfulness will not know about the righteous things you do.” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-ellipsis]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: my prayer comes before you
OccurrenceNote: The writer praying to Yahweh is spoken of as if the prayer itself goes to speak with Yahweh. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Why do you hide your face from me?
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of the writer feeling like God has rejected or abandoned him as if God were hiding his face or physically turning away from the writer. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: Your angry actions have passed over me
OccurrenceNote: This speaks of God punishing the writer as if God’s actions are a large wave rising out of the sea that fall on and crush the writer. Alternate translation: “It is as if your angry actions crush me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: your terrifying deeds have annihilated me
OccurrenceNote: This exaggeration speaks about God punishing the writer as if God has completely destroyed the writer. Alternate translation: “the terrifying things you do have destroyed me” or “the terrifying things you do have almost destroyed me” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-hyperbole]])

GLQuote: They surround me like water all the day long
OccurrenceNote: The writer compares God’s “angry actions” and “terrifying deeds” to a flood of water. Alternate translation: “All day long they threaten to destroy me like a flood” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-simile]])

GLQuote: they have all encircled me
OccurrenceNote: The writer speaks of God’s “angry actions” and “terrifying deeds” as if they were enemies who were trying to capture and kill him. Alternate translation: “they have surrounded me like enemy soldiers” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: My only acquaintance is the darkness
OccurrenceNote: This speaks about darkness as if it were a person that could be friends with someone else. The writer is emphasizing that he feels completely alone. Alternate translation: “Everywhere I go it is dark” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]])

GLQuote: acts of covenant faithfulness
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea with an adjective. Alternate translation: “faithful acts” or “loving acts” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-abstractnouns]])

GLQuote: Covenant faithfulness has been established forever
OccurrenceNote: God always doing what he promised to do is spoken of as if his faithfulness were a building that God has built and made firm. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “You will always be faithful because of your covenant with us” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: your truthfulness you have established in the heavens
OccurrenceNote: God always doing what he promised to do is spoken of as if his faithfulness were a building that God has built and made firm. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I have made a covenant with my chosen one
OccurrenceNote: You can make explicit that “chosen one” refers to David. Alternate translation: “I made a promise to David, the one I chose” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]])

GLQuote: I will establish your descendants forever
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh always causing one of David’s descendants to be king is spoken of as if David’s descendants are a building that Yahweh will build and make firm. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: I will establish your throne through all generations
OccurrenceNote: Here “throne” represents the power to rule as king. The psalmist speaks of God promising that one of David’s descendants will always rule as king as if God will build David’s throne and make it firm. Alternate translation: “I will make sure that one of your descendants will rule as king over every generation of my people” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: The heavens praise
OccurrenceNote: Here “heavens” represents those who are in heaven. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: your truthfulness is praised in the assembly of the holy ones
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **truthfulness**, you could express the same idea with a verbal form such as “you always do what you promise to do.” This can also be stated in active form. Alternate translation: “The assembly of the holy ones praises you because you always do what you promise to do” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: For who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of the gods is like Yahweh?
OccurrenceNote: Both questions mean the same thing. The writer is using question to emphasize that there in no one in heaven like Yahweh. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-parallelism]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: sons of the gods
OccurrenceNote: Here “sons of” means having the characteristics of. This is a way of referring to other spiritual beings that live in heaven. Alternate translation: “angels” or “divine beings” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-idiom]])

GLQuote: He is a God who is greatly honored in the council of the holy ones
OccurrenceNote: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: “The council of the holy ones greatly honors God” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-activepassive]])

GLQuote: who is strong like you, Yahweh?
OccurrenceNote: The writer asks the question to emphasize there is no one as strong as Yahweh. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-rquestion]])

GLQuote: Your truthfulness surrounds you
OccurrenceNote: Yahweh always dong what he promises to do is spoken of as if his truthfulness were a cloak or garment that wraps around him. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

GLQuote: You crushed Rahab as one who is killed
OccurrenceNote: The word “Rahab” here refers to a monster of the sea. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-explicit]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/translate-names]])

GLQuote: with your strong arm
OccurrenceNote: Here “arm” represents power. Alternate translation: “with your great power” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: the north and the south
OccurrenceNote: The writer uses the words “north” and “south” together to mean that God created everything everywhere. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-merism]])

GLQuote: Tabor and Hermon rejoice in your name
OccurrenceNote: Tabor is a mountain southwest of the sea of Galilee and Hermon is a mountain northeast of the sea of Galilee. The writer describes these mountains as if they were persons who could rejoice. Alternate translation: “It is as if Mount Tabor and Mount Hermon were rejoicing in your name” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-personification]] and [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/translate-names]])

GLQuote: in your name
OccurrenceNote: Here “name” represents the whole person. Alternate translation: “in you” (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])

GLQuote: You have a mighty arm and a strong hand, and your right hand is high
OccurrenceNote: The words “mighty arm,” “strong hand,” and “right hand” all represent God’s power. (See: [[rc://en/ta/man/translate/figs-metonymy]])
